articles.title: Microsoft shuts the door on The Garage, the central program behind its hackathon and maker spaces
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft is winding down The Garage as a companywide program, ending a 17-year run for the effort that gave employees space and tools for side projects and ran the company’s Global Hackathon, according to an internal FAQ viewed by GeekWire.

The program, with a flagship location on Microsoft’s Redmond campus and more than a dozen other sites from Vancouver, B.C., to Beijing, has been a showcase for the culture change that Satya Nadella led after becoming CEO in 2014.

In the FAQ, Microsoft says the experimentation that started in dedicated programs and spaces like The Garage now happens “every day within each of our teams,” as employees build new skills and adopt new tools in their regular work. The company says it is “reinventing how we foster innovation, learning, and experimentation” across Microsoft.
The move comes as Microsoft spends heavily on AI, much of it for data centers and other infrastructure, while cutting costs and jobs in other parts of the business.

“We regularly evaluate how we use our physical spaces to best support our employees, customers and partners,” a Microsoft spokesperson said in a statement. “As part of that ongoing work, we’re making changes to some Garage spaces. Innovation and a builder mindset remain central to how we work every day.”
The company declined to comment further, including on the effect on Garage employees.

The Garage will no longer operate “as a centralized function,” according to the FAQ, and the impact on each physical space “will vary by location.” Some Garage spaces could be restricted as early as Friday, Oct. 23. Neither the FAQ nor Microsoft’s statement says which spaces are affected, including the flagship location in Redmond. Employees can’t take equipment, tools or materials with them.
The future of the Global Hackathon is also unsettled. The FAQ says the hackathon team is “reimagining the program” and that Microsoft will have more to share later.
Microsoft’s public Garage website, which showcased hackathon projects and experimental apps, was redirecting to the Microsoft homepage as of Tuesday morning.

From Office Labs to companywide: The Garage started in 2009 inside Microsoft’s Office Labs group in Redmond, with the slogan “Doers. Not Talkers.” The idea was to support employees who were already building their own projects, rather than collecting ideas and funding the most popular ones.

The program took on a bigger role under Nadella. In July 2014, The Garage ran Microsoft’s first companywide hackathon, which drew more than 11,000 registrants from 80 countries. The event became an annual fixture of Microsoft’s culture.

The Garage also released experimental apps to the public, including Mouse without Borders, a tool for controlling multiple PCs with one keyboard and mouse, and Arrow Launcher, which became Microsoft Launcher for Android.
As of this year, Microsoft listed Garage locations in 15 regions, including Redmond, Vancouver, B.C., the Bay Area, New York City, Dublin, Israel, India and Beijing.

Employee reaction: On Blind, the anonymous workplace app that verifies users’ employers, a post titled “Amy kills the Garage” drew more than 70 comments. The poster attributed the move to cost-cutting by Microsoft CFO Amy Hood.
Another employee wrote that The Garage was where they met their friends on campus and made connections that advanced their career.
“The Garage offices were one of the last few cool things about Microsoft,” one commenter wrote.

articles.title: Autonomous flight startup Reliable Robotics opens Seattle area radar hub as valuation tops $1 billion
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Aviation startup Reliable Robotics is opening a new engineering hub in the Seattle area, establishing a radar research and development center in Bothell.

The Mountain View, Calif.-based company also announced Tuesday that it has raised $115 million , pushing its valuation above $1 billion. The funding will help expand its aircraft fleet, production facilities and engineering team as it works toward federal certification of its autonomous flight technology.

Reliable’s new office in the Bothell Highlands north of Seattle will open with about 25 employees and serve as its Radar Center of Excellence, a facility for developing and testing systems designed to help aircraft detect and avoid other aircraft. The company plans to grow the team and is heavily recruiting in the region, including roles across radar, embedded software, flight controls, guidance and navigation, simulation and systems engineering.
The expansion adds another player to the Seattle area’s growing mix of aerospace, robotics and autonomous systems companies.

Last month, GeekWire reported that San Diego-based Shield AI selected Des Moines, Wash. as the production and engineering hub for its X-BAT, an AI-piloted aircraft designed to take off and land vertically. The heavily-funded company is planning a 420,000-square-foot manufacturing and engineering facility and says it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the region by the early 2030s.

Reliable is developing systems that can automate aircraft operations, including engine startup, taxiing, takeoff and landing. Its longer-term ambitions include enabling aircraft to fly without a pilot aboard, with remote operators overseeing flights from the ground. The company is working toward certification from the Federal Aviation Administration.

Founded by former SpaceX engineers in 2017, Reliable has spent nearly a decade developing technology designed to work with existing aircraft rather than requiring entirely new planes. Its initial system is intended to keep a pilot in the cockpit while automating key flight operations, with more advanced levels of autonomy planned over time.
The 250-person company’s latest financing, including $90 million led by Nimble Partners and a $25 million term loan from Silicon Valley Bank, brings total funding to $380 million.
The company’s new Bothell lab will bring together engineers to design, build and test radar systems, including its active electronically scanned array air-to-air radar.
The technology is intended to support detect-and-avoid capabilities that would help autonomous aircraft safely operate in the national airspace alongside conventional planes.

“Seattle represents the past, present and future of aviation. For decades, engineers here have developed aircraft and systems that change how the world connects,” said Chris Schulenberg, Reliable’s vice president of programs, said in the company’s announcement. “By expanding into the Pacific Northwest, Reliable is uniting the tech talent in Silicon Valley with the aviation expertise of Seattle.”
The Bothell office — located at 21222 30th Dr SE — will be led by Schulenberg and Marc Pos , a senior technical fellow focused on radar who previously spent more than two decades at Honeywell.

“Radar development is a hands-on process,” said Pos in a release. “By bringing a team together in a centralized lab and engineering environment, with all of the resources we need at our fingertips, we can move from design through development and testing with the rigor, speed and precision unique to Reliable.
Reliable also plans to expand its engineering operations in San Diego, where it will focus on aviation autonomy for military applications.

The two offices bring the company’s footprint to five locations, joining its headquarters and aircraft hangars in California and the operating hub of its subsidiary airline, Reliable Airlines, in Albuquerque, N.M.

articles.title: Amazon plans record 300k holiday hires as the rest of retail pulls back
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Amazon says it plans to hire more than 300,000 people for seasonal, part-time and full-time roles across its U.S. operations this holiday season, an increase of 20% from last year and its largest holiday hiring target on record.
The increase reflects a mix of factors, including new sites opening across the country as Amazon expands its operations network, a spokesperson said in response to questions.

Amazon is moving in the opposite direction from the rest of retail. Retailers added the fewest seasonal workers since 2008 last holiday season, and outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas expects even fewer this year , citing automation and uncertain holiday spending as tariffs keep prices high.

UPS plans to hire more than 100,000 seasonal workers , about 9% fewer than last year, according to Reuters , after cutting the volume it handles for Amazon, which now delivers most of its own packages. Target and Walmart haven’t announced national hiring goals.

Amazon’s sales volume has picked up this year. Worldwide paid units, a measure of items sold on Amazon, grew 17% year-over-year in the second quarter, up from 12% a year earlier, according to its second-quarter earnings release .
CEO Andy Jassy said in the earnings release that Amazon set record delivery speeds for Prime members in the first half of the year, with “over 40% more items delivered same-day or overnight.”

Amazon also said Tuesday that seasonal employees who work at least 30 hours a week will be eligible for healthcare from their first day, starting Jan. 1. Seasonal workers previously had to wait 90 days for coverage, meaning that many holiday hires could finish their seasonal jobs before they became eligible.
The change doesn’t apply to the upcoming peak season, but workers hired over the holidays who are still in qualifying roles on Jan. 1 will gain coverage that day, the company said.

Seasonal workers earn an average of $20 an hour. Full-time operations employees start at a minimum of $20 an hour, and average pay across Amazon’s operations workforce is nearly $24, following a pay increase Amazon announced last month .

The hiring push for Amazon’s fulfillment centers and delivery stations comes as the company shrinks its corporate workforce. Amazon cut 16,000 corporate jobs in January, bringing its total reductions to about 30,000 since October 2025.
Amazon had about 1.6 million employees as of June 30, up 3% from a year earlier, excluding contractors and temporary workers. The company reports third-quarter results Oct. 29.

articles.title: From dishes to diapers: Seattle home-help startup Rosie raises $7M, eyes Austin and S.F. in 2027
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Mitra Raman was making dinner one night, watching her young son play with the babysitter, when she realized she wanted to trade places. “I’m his parent,” she recalls thinking. “I want to play with him. I want to spend time with him.”

That moment was one of the sparks for Rosie , a Seattle startup that sends caregivers into homes to do a mix of childcare and household work, from folding laundry and resetting the kitchen to watching the kids. The name is an homage to the robot housekeeper on the classic TV cartoon show “The Jetsons.”

Raman, Rosie’s CEO and a former Amazon engineer, co-founded the company last year with Chief Operating Officer Karthika Shankar , who spent more than 12 years at Amazon, managing recruiting teams and leading hiring and onboarding programs.

The founders, both working moms, saw a gap in the market between dedicated childcare and housekeeping. By giving parents what some customers call a “mom body double,” they wanted to free up time for the things parents actually want to do, like playing with their kids.
Rosie serves nearly 300 families in the Seattle area with a full-time team of four plus a few part-time staff and more than 100 caregivers it calls Pros.

The news: The company announced Tuesday that it has raised $7 million across two rounds led by Bling Capital and Reach Capital . Rosie says it reached seven-figure annual recurring revenue within eight months. It plans to use the funding to fuel its growth and expansion, starting with a launch in Austin in early 2027, followed by San Francisco later in the year.

Other investors include Graham & Walker ( Leslie Feinzaig ), Marketplace Capital , Ingeborg Investments , Precursor Ventures , Mother Ventures and Yonder Ventures . Angel investors include DoorDash co-founder Evan Moore and Seattle startup leader Aviel Ginzburg of Founders’ Co-op and Foundations.

How it works: Families buy a monthly membership : $250 for eight hours, $500 for 16 hours or $750 for 24 hours, with extra hours billed at $32 each and no long-term contract. Most families set up a weekly schedule with the same Pro, according to Rosie’s website , and they can also book same-day help through the app or by text.
Families can add Pros they like to a “bench” of regulars and book them directly. “Who shows up actually matters,” Raman said. “It’s not interchangeable supply.”
Rosie matches families with Pros and handles scheduling and payments. It runs separate apps for families and Pros , both released earlier this year.

Rosie uses AI to help with the logistics, keeping track of each family’s routines, preferences and favorite Pros, and handling matching and scheduling behind the scenes. The underlying AI system is called Jetson, continuing the theme.

But the founders say they’re deliberate about where they use AI. Raman said the company applies it where it clearly saves time or where it can be about 99% sure it’s right, because parents and Pros don’t have time to wade through AI output they don’t need.
Learning the job: In the company’s early days, Raman and Shankar worked as Rosie’s first Pros, watching kids, folding laundry, wrapping gifts and organizing garages in customers’ homes.

They also did the intake visits themselves, sitting at kitchen tables and walking through homes, where parents often apologized for the mess. Shankar recalled reassuring them that this was normal: “You don’t need to show me some Pinterest-perfect house.”

The founders said the work showed them that every household runs differently, down to how a family wants its laundry folded or its dishes washed. That shaped how Rosie uses AI: to remember each home’s routines and pass them along to the Pros who work there.
GeekWire first took note of Rosie in July 2025, when it was still in a private beta.

What Pros do, and how they’re vetted: Pros will tidy up, but Rosie draws the line at deep cleaning. (Its FAQ says no scrubbing toilets.) Shankar said the company looked at what a house cleaner typically does and built its service around everything else: unloading the dishwasher, putting things away, taking out the trash, sorting outgrown kids’ clothes.
Driving children is handled case by case, with checks of a Pro’s driving record and insurance.
Vetting Pros draws in part on Shankar’s background at Amazon, where much of her recruiting work was high-volume hiring for Amazon’s field operations, rather than corporate or tech jobs.

Pros go through an online intake, identity verification, a background check and reference checks run by AI. Then comes an in-person assessment at Rosie’s office on Capitol Hill, where prospective Pros fold laundry, load a dishwasher and work through childcare scenarios, using a stash of laundry that includes Raman’s kids’ old onesies. The company is now testing virtual assessments as it scales.

A long line of attempts: The best-known name in the category is Care.com , which bills itself as the largest online marketplace for family care. Families search profiles of babysitters, nannies, housekeepers and other caregivers and make their own hires.
Startups that tried a more hands-on approach have had mixed results.
Homejoy, an on-demand cleaning startup that raised about $40 million, shut down in 2015 , with its CEO citing lawsuits over whether its cleaners should have been classified as employees.

Hello Alfred, which sent weekly “home managers” to handle errands and chores, raised a $40 million Series B in 2018 and launched in Seattle the next year, selling its service through apartment buildings. Its home managers were full-time employees.

The founders say Rosie is built differently. Families pay a monthly membership up front, and the model depends on the same Pros returning to the same homes each week, not one-off jobs filled by whoever is available. “Rosie does not exist without our Pros,” Shankar said.

The workforce model: Rosie classifies its Pros as independent contractors, paid per session through the company’s app. Rosie sets what families pay and what Pros earn, matches Pros with families and clarifies the tasks for each session before it’s booked.
Asked why Rosie’s Pros aren’t classified as employees, Raman said they have “full flexibility to decide what they do, what session they take, when they take it.”
“We’re not going to tell you where and what to work,” she said. “You decide.”

Rosie’s Pros include college students and part-time professionals looking for flexible work. Pay is set by an algorithm that weighs factors including the length of a session, the number of children, the type of work and whether the Pro is returning to a family they’ve worked with before.

Shankar said part-time Pros might earn a couple hundred dollars a week, while those who work more can make $500 to $1,000 a week. Recent Rosie job listings in the Seattle area have advertised $22 to $24 an hour, plus bonuses.

From Seattle to Austin and S.F.: When the service launched in January, Rosie opened to anyone in the Seattle area to see where demand and supply would come from. Pros mostly want steady routines close to home, and many in Seattle rely on public transit, Raman said.
TR=hat open approach meant some families and Pros lived far apart. In new cities, the company plans to launch neighborhood by neighborhood, starting where it expects to find its first Pros.
Austin and San Francisco share Seattle’s mix of tech-friendly, dual-income families, plus nearby universities where Rosie can recruit Pros.

Raman said the company chose to launch next in Austin partly because it’s different from Seattle in other ways. One difference: People there drive more and rely less on public transit, which changes how Pros get to families.

Rosie is hiring an in-person city general manager in Austin, according to its job listings , along with a senior software engineer and a “forward deployed engineer” for operations. That posting describes a goal of “100% AI-managed matching and scheduling with a small, deliberate human-in-the-loop.”

The bigger idea: The founders see childcare as the entry point to a broader platform. Some families are already booking Pros through Rosie for pet care and companionship for older relatives, Shankar said, and others are asking for help with errands and driving.
Raman described the overall thesis: “If you trust us with your kids,” she said, “you’ll trust us then with everything else.”

articles.title: Seattle ag-tech startup Carbon Robotics reduces workforce, citing economic conditions
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Carbon Robotics , the Seattle-based agricultural technology startup known for its AI-powered, laser-weeding farm implements, has trimmed its workforce.
The company did not disclose the total number of layoffs, but confirmed to GeekWire on Monday that the cuts affected employees across multiple departments both in the U.S. and internationally.

Carbon Robotics currently employs 275 people worldwide, according to Brett Goodwin, vice president of marketing, who attributed the decision to a need to “realign costs due to broader economic conditions.”

The cuts come after a period of rapid momentum for the startup. The company raised $20 million last year to support the development of an undisclosed AI-powered farm robot. Carbon also unveiled an autonomous tractor kit in 2025.

The company’s signature product is its LaserWeeder, a machine which can be pulled behind a tractor and uses AI to detect and map plants in fields and then target and eliminate weeds with lasers. The most recent iteration is the LaserWeeder G2 .
Founded in 2018 and led by CEO Paul Mikesell , Carbon Robotics has raised about $177 million to date from investors including BOND, NVentures, and Anthos Capital.

In a recent interview with AgFunder, Mikesell noted that the startup crossed the $100 million revenue threshold, stating, “We intend to keep scaling from there — it’s our intention to get to the point that we’re an independently publicly traded company, so that would involve going through an IPO.”

Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the U.S. secretary of health and human services, earlier this year touted Carbon Robotics’ machines on an episode of “The Joe Rogan Experience” as a possible solution in cutting pesticide use.
Carbon Robotics was named Next Tech Titan at the 2026 GeekWire Awards earlier this year. The company is currently ranked No. 8 on the GeekWire 200 index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

articles.title: State Lawmaker, SDOT Director Clash Over Aurora Avenue Overhaul
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Slow progress in advancing plans for the future of Aurora Avenue appears to be leading to mounting tensions between state legislators and the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). Those tensions came to a head in an email exchange just this month between Representative Julia Reed (D-36th LD, Queen Anne) and Acting SDOT Director Angela Brady, a copy of which was obtained by The Urbanist.

The spicy exchange comes more than four years after state lawmakers set aside $50 million for improvements to Seattle's deadliest roadway, which also operates as State Route 99 for its entire length within city limits. An earmark spearheaded by former state Senator Reuven Carlyle, who referred to Aurora as a "scar, ripping through the center of our city", those funds were intended to be a down payment on a fully transformed corridor that he compared to the Champs-Élysées.

But things remain stuck in the planning stage, despite legislative direction in 2022 targeting upgrades between N 90th Street and N 105th Street as a demonstration project that would pave the way for changes elsewhere. SDOT ultimately did not follow that direction, setting up a safety project to look at the entire corridor between South Lake Union and N 145th Street and looping in King County Metro and Seattle Public Utilities in a move that was certain to make the project harder to implement.

Meanwhile, transportation advocates have shifted their focus further south, to the stretch of Aurora Avenue that divides sections of the Fremont neighborhood from each other. Reconnect Fremont, a project of the Aurora Reimagined Coalition (ARC), represents a push for new marked crossings and bus stops that will start to stitch the neighborhood back together. Families with kids at B.F. Day Elementary School who live on the east side of Aurora currently have to use an overpass at N 41st Street to access school, something that doesn't really work for households who get around by bike.
"We want to cut through the endless studies and build momentum through action," ARC stated in a blog post on Reconnecting Fremont earlier this year.

That goal appears to be shared by Rep. Reed, who serves as Vice Chair of the House transportation committee. Following up on an August call that took place with SDOT and staff from Mayor Katie Wilson's office, Rep. Reed wrote to SDOT Director Brady on October 2 – more than a month after that call took place.

"Wanted to check in from our call in August about looking for the City to take action on the highly needed demonstration projects connecting Fremont across Aurora," Reed wrote. She referenced a commitment made during the calll to set up a meeting between ARC and the consultant team currently looking at potential upgrades to Aurora, from the firm Parametrix. "[I]n our call, the Mayor’s office committed to looking at these projects and taking more urgent action to implement them or at least coming up with a plan in the short term – has that happened?"

Brady's response skirted around the issue of near-term improvements along Aurora in Fremont, instead reiterating the work the SDOT already has done to improve safety on the corridor without directly utilizing state funding.

"We share the sense of urgency that Aurora Ave N is in need of improvements now," Brady wrote. "Over the last three years, we have expanded bus lane operations, installed No Turn on Red and Leading Pedestrian Intervals (LPIs), repainted and widened all crosswalks, added center medians and hardened centerlines to reduce turning conflicts, and updated signal timing corridor-wide to increase pedestrian crossing times. We are currently wrapping up construction of a new signal at N 137 th St and completing designs for another package of additional near-term improvements."

But Brady, who took over as Interim SDOT Director in January after a long stint in the city's Office of the Waterfront & Civic Projects, also told Reed that the department has been having a hard time figuring out how to use the $50 million in funding from the 2022 Move Ahead Washington (MAW) transportation package.

"Generally, we have found that the MAW funds have not been easy for SDOT to use for near-term work. They are administered by WSDOT Local Programs similar to a state grant, making them challenging for the City to pivot and use quickly," Brady said. "Seattle is currently exploring various scenarios for sequencing MAW dollars – including near term improvements and a more focused, targeted approach to longer-term improvements. We look forward to discussing those options with you ahead of session."

Reed wrote back visibly frustrated, framing Brady as backing off a promise to set up the direct meeting between ARC and Parametrix, and a commitment to provide concrete next steps on quick build projects that could help to reconnect Fremont.

"I’m sure it is not the city’s intention to go back on its word to a sitting representative and member of the Transportation committee — especially since as we discussed the heart of this problem is a lack of trust in SDOT to administer the state funds effectively," Reed wrote. "I’ve worked in city government a long time so I speak roundabout email as well as anyone. Please do not spray water on my inbox and then try to convince me it is raining."

Reed was even more blunt in an aside in a follow-up email directed to Alex Hudson, at the time Katie Wilson's Senior Policy Advisor on Transportation & Livability. (Hudson has since spent several weeks filling in as Wilson's Interim Press Secretary, but is now returning to her prior role.)

"If the city does not plan to keep the commitments we discussed then I will note that 1) the City is not a trustworthy partner than can be relied on to do what it says it will do when it comes to Transportation work, which will just for the record have an influence on the level of effort I want to put in to advocate for city priorities at the state level and 2) recommend to Chair Fey that the $50 million could be better used in a more directed fashion to improve near term conditions on Aurora," Reed wrote.

Reed, responding to an inquiry about the email exchange via text, made it clear that funding for Aurora remains a priority for her office, but reiterated her frustration with the City of Seattle's pace of action.

"I will say for the record I have no wish to diminish funding for Aurora or to endanger the set aside which goes back to Reuven Carlyle days. But I do want SDOT to take ARC seriously and to take me seriously when I say that waiting two more years before you even think about doing a project is not acceptable," Reed wrote. "This is about trust as much as anything, and following through on the small commitments and pushing forward the bigger demonstration projects is how SDOT builds trust with me and the community that we’re really on the same page."

"Also I commend all the hard work ARC members have put in as volunteers to create a reasonable, achievable, and practical vision," Reed continued. "I don’t think they’re asking for that much and I think city departments should be doing cartwheels of joy to have community members who are so organically engaged at a time when SDOT routinely spends thousands trying to produce even a fraction of this engagement."

Since the email exchange, Reed and Brady met one-on-one this past Friday, a meeting that reportedly went positively. SDOT spokesperson Ethan Bergerson portrayed the department as making progress on Aurora in a statement provided to The Urbanist in the wake of that meeting.

"Acting Director Angela Brady and SDOT staff have a commitment, responsibility, and desire to improve safety on Aurora Ave N. We greatly value Representative Reed’s partnership on this important project and appreciate the work of advocates in continuing to elevate and participate in solutions for the critical needs on Aurora Ave N," Bergerson wrote. "There was a misunderstanding about a commitment made in a meeting regarding the Aurora Ave Project. Now that we’re aware of the misunderstanding, we are scheduling a meeting in November between members of the Aurora Reimagined Coalition and our consultant team."

Bergerson noted that SDOT is working toward wrapping up the planning phase on the Aurora project by next year, a condition of state grant funding the city has already received. $3 million allocated by the legislature remains unobligated, out of the city's reach. Receiving the remaining $44 million will require direct coordination with legislators.

Whether the Aurora project can finally see some forward momentum remains to be seen. And Reed's email exchange voiced concerns that many transportation advocates have raised around the slow pace of work to tackle some of Seattle's most dangerous streets, with the goings-on inside the city's insular transportation department seemingly impenetrable even to a state legislator. Though Mayor Katie Wilson issued an executive order in August directing SDOT to accelerate work on Vision Zero projects, many of the highest-profile corridor overhauls included in the 2024 Seattle Transportation Levy remain in early stages.

"Aurora Avenue is Seattle's most dangerous street. It is polluted, noisy, and divides our neighborhoods. Representative Reed is a strong and steadfast supporter of ARC and our mission to change Aurora for the better. She has worked tirelessly alongside her constituents to ensure SDOT's plan for Aurora is truly transformational," Aurora Reimagined Coalition member Carlo Alcantara told The Urbanist . "Like Rep Reed, ARC would like to see more near-term action on demonstration projects like Reconnect Fremont. These demonstration projects start to reimagine Aurora as a neighborhood main street rather than a highway bisecting our neighborhoods."

articles.title: Changing the Zoning for most of Seattle
articles.author: Ross Bleakney
paras: “ Neighborhood Residential ” (previously called “Single-Family”) is the most common zoning type in Seattle. It makes up about 2/3 of the land zoned for development in the city. This is where we have the greatest potential for improving population density and affordability in Seattle. Here is a proposal for simple changes that could make a huge difference. This zoning type used to be three minimum lot sizes. Now there’s only one: 5,000 square feet . Along with lowering the size limit for new lots, other rules are now a bit more liberal. While these changes are laudable, they are still complicated and aren’t as liberal as what Spokane has . I believe we can do better.

We should get rid of minimum lot sizes in the city. As long as a builder adheres to other regulations they should be free to build small-lot homes, like row houses or skinny houses . Some people will still want bigger lots. But it is quite likely this would give a lot more people the opportunity to own both a home and the land under it.

The city restricts both the size of the lots, the dimensions of the structure, and the number of units. This is labeled “ Maximum Density ” in the code. We should eliminate these limits. Rules and regulations should be based on the structure itself, not how many people can live there. I can understand why people don’t want to see a big building next to them. But if you can build a three-story house next to me, I don’t care how many units it has. It might as well be a short apartment or condo. This would also allow for a lot more houses to be converted to apartments. Limit the dimensions of the structure, not the number of units.

There are also rules about “ lot coverage ” or what portion of the land can be covered by the structure. Typically this limits the structure to using half the lot. These rules are designed in part to limit water runoff. But the structure should simply be considered as part of the rules governing impervious surfaces . A house taking up 60% of the lot is basically the same as a house taking up 30% and parking taking up 30%. As long as the developer adheres to the stormwater code, both should be allowed.

Parking requirements push up the cost of new construction. As a result, this pushes up the cost of buying a new place or renting a new unit. But since new units impact the cost of existing units, all renters are hurt by the parking requirement. In contrast, existing owners aren’t effected by the regulations since they already own their property. Additional parking in a neighborhood can be considered a benefit to everyone who lives in the neighborhood (which is why the requirement was enacted in the first place). People who live there or visit are less likely to park on the street. But since existing owners pay nothing for this benefit, the burden falls entirely on those who rent or are looking to buy. If you believe that parking is a public good (and I don’t) then everyone should chip in for public parking lots. Regardless, we should remove all parking requirements for new housing.

Floor Area Ratio or FAR is the ratio of a building’s total floor area to the size of the piece of land upon which it is built. A FAR of 1.0 means that you can cover the entire lot area with a building that is one story high. It also means that you can cover half the lot with a two-story building (or a third of the lot with three-story building, etc.). A ratio of 0.5 means that you can only cover half the lot with a one-story building (or one quarter of the lot with a two-story building). Likewise, a ratio or 2.0 means that you can cover the entire lot with a building that is two stories high (or half the lot with a four-story building, etc.).

The land zoned neighborhood residential is limited to three stories. Thus any FAR less than 3.0 limits construction. While the FAR limit specified by the city for neighborhood residential varies quite a bit depending on various factors, it is always less than 3.0. This limits the amount of housing that can be built. FAR regulations should be eliminated for this zoning type (if not others).

A “setback” is the minimum distance which a building or other structure must be set back from the property line. There are rules that apply to the front, rear and each side. The front setback is typically based on aesthetics, which are debatable. Paris has no setbacks. Montreal has small setbacks. These are widely considered extremely attractive cities.

Other setbacks are based on the interests of immediate neighbors. In a lot of cases, people don’t want the new owner to build right up to the property line. But side setbacks and rear setbacks should be negotiable. The neighbors — the only people who would actually be impacted by development in those areas — should be able to allow it. Just as you can buy “air rights” over a property, the neighbor should be able to sell development rights right up to the edge of property. There are plenty of people — whose house is already in the middle of the lot — that wouldn’t mind such development at all. Just as importantly, this would also row houses — with the houses right next to each other — in any subdivision.

These changes are relatively simple. They would not alter the height limits that exist. Yet they would change the rules that govern the vast majority of land that can be developed in the city. A lot more people would be able to afford to live in Seattle.

articles.title: $pent Studios settles into E Pike with $10 bins, a papier-mâché jacket, and big plans beyond the racks
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: Hudson Wakefield’s mom was sitting a few feet away, pricing jeans as he explained how all of this started. She’s the reason, really. When he was in elementary school, she’d take him thrifting, and the habit stuck long before fashion did.
“I wasn’t really super big into fashion, but I just loved thrifting and finding stuff for me,” Wakefield, 24, tells CHS.
These days, that habit fills a Capitol HIll storefront.
$pent Studios had been growing underground a few blocks away on 12th Ave and is now in the heart of the party on E Pike, where it replaced a candle bar on the block home to the Comet .

Wakefield figured he was headed toward film in high school. Then the pandemic hit, the free time piled up, and he and his friends were thrifting more than ever. Along the way, he kept finding pieces people had tossed for a hole or a stain that were still too good for the dump. He grabbed his sister’s sewing machine and started patching.
“Sewing, it’s like therapeutic,” he said. He’d like the custom, one-of-one work to someday match the volume of vintage on the floor. Right now, he admits, he’s in business-running mode.

The 12th Ave basement was where $pent grew the most, Wakefield said, with the shop and concerts sharing the same space. But the landlord wanted a single tenant to take over the whole basement, and $pent only occupied two of the roughly 10 rooms. Taking on the rest was out of range.
“We were basically getting kicked out of there, and I got this just in time,” he said. The E Pike spot was the better location anyway.

People will says things are overpriced, no matter what, Wakefield says, even at $5. He points to the $10 bin, where he said you will find jackets that would run $20 to $25 at Goodwill . Sourcing cheaply from thrift stores lets him keep prices down, and he tells people who sell to the shop that he’s offering a fair price, not lowballing them to mark it up tenfold.
“We’re just giving a fair price for us so we can be able to sell it for a good price for the customer, but then also try to be as fair to the person selling as possible,” he said.
The racks are organized by type, with $pent’s own pieces mixed right in. Flip through and you might hit Gucci, then Balenciaga, then a $pent piece, then a random $15 vintage tee.
“You never know what’s next when you’re looking at the rack,” Wakefield said.

Ask him what a first-timer should see, and Wakefield points to what he’s been calling the papier-mâché jacket. It’s not really wearable. It’s more art than clothing, and it came out of a fashion show $pent staged in April with Goodwill at its Dearborn store.

That partnership had an unlikely start. Wakefield and a group of models walked into the Goodwill unannounced and staged a fashion show in the middle of the store while staff were rotating stock. He half expected someone to call the police. Instead, Goodwill told him they didn’t love the lack of permission, but they liked the idea. About six months later, they made it official, with every piece shopped from Goodwill and reworked.
What makes a thrifted find a $pent piece? “I gotta do something to it,” Wakefield said. Sometimes that’s a full rework. Sometimes it’s printing a logo on something that’s already great.

$pent’s old space doubled as an all-ages DIY venue. That won’t work on E Pike, Wakefield said, but pop-ups, meet-and-greets, and small after-parties are still in the plan. Bigger shows will move to venues around the city. The shop’s next fashion show is set for the Comet with DJs, and it’s $pent’s first 21-and-over event. Another collaboration with Neumos across the street is in the works for November.
He still wants to keep putting on for the under-21 crowd. “I know how it is,” he said.

This summer’s Capitol Hill Block Party came with its own lesson. The store was largely fenced off, but organizers gave $pent a free booth inside the grounds. The shop made good money, met a lot of people, and the crew watched the headliner from the front steps. Wakefield hopes to be more involved in coming years.
“I feel like we could be a valuable part of that somehow, more than just popping up,” he said.

$pent is part of a robust thrift, vintage, and consignment community around Capitol Hill including Break Away and Magpie Thrift in the old Red Light space on Broadway. Wakefield puts his shop in the middle of the scale. $pent has sold pieces for as much as $7,000. It also has the $10 bin, and sometimes things go out the door for free.

These blocks of the Pike/Pine nightlife core also have made spaces for a diverse pocket of the fashion economy. Longtimers like Veridis and BAIT are being joined by new projects like the Furesh furry store while Sergius & Bacchus has new energy in a new space in the old Shikorina bakeshop space on E Pike next to Retail Therapy and the Slow Dance vintage and consignment shop. The Out of the Closet thrift shop helps round out the offerings.

Moving to E Pike has meant moving far more volume, so Wakefield is out, sourcing every day. He goes to estate sales and thrift stores, and he has even pulled a few things from abandoned buildings –“a little sketchy,” he said. The best stuff, though, comes from people walking in to sell or trade. A batch of leather jackets is about to hit the floor.

Black Friday sales, more shows, and a fully stocked store, for starters. Longer term, Wakefield wants $pent to be more than a clothing store. He’s thinking furniture, food, and a revival of the $pent energy drinks the brand released in a small run last year. He would also like more real estate in the neighborhood.
“There’s a lot more coming,” Wakefield said.
$pent Studios is now open at 910 E Pike. Learn more at spentstudios.com .

articles.title: Seattle set to pass new rules giving people living in RVs a parking permit — if they accept shelter services
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Tuesday afternoon, the Seattle City Council is expected to approve a “Vehicle Resident Assistance Program” including a new permit system for people already living in their vehicles, funding for safe lots and secure vehicle storage, and new overnight parking bans across the city. The program will be funded by $5 million already earmarked for homelessness services.
Councilmember Dan Strauss introduced the six-part legislative package this summer.

The cornerstone of the plan is a permitting system for motor homes and travel trailers that is hoped to move more people into more permanent shelter. Eligible vehicle residents identified through a one-time Human Services Department census can obtain a permit allowing overnight parking strictly within designated industrial zones, provided they work with caseworkers and follow neighborhood cleanliness rules. Permits will be revoked if an occupant declines six offers of appropriate shelter.
Unpermitted vehicles would be restricted to two hours of street parking, barred from overnight parking, and subject to immediate impoundment without prior notice.
The permitting and impoundment regulations apply only to “motor homes and travel trailers,” not passenger cars, vans, or SUVs.

Councilmembers are weighing three proposed amendments. Amendment A, sponsored by Councilmember Eddie Lin , would expand the Vehicle Residency Implementation Review Workgroup to include contracted service and outreach providers while broadening its scope to examine warning procedures, equity, and operational readiness. Another proposed Lin amendment directs the workgroup to establish ongoing monitoring metrics, conduct a citywide census of vehicle residents, and deliver annual evaluation reports to the council. Finally, Amendment C, sponsored by Councilmember Maritz Rivera , mandates the revocation of a permit if the holder is convicted of, or enters a diversion agreement for offenses involving drug dealing, sex trafficking, commercial sexual exploitation of children, or prostitution-related loitering.

For unpermitted RVs and trailers, new restrictions taking effect next April will cap street parking at two hours citywide and ban overnight parking between midnight and 6 AM, backed by impoundment authority following a 90-day warning period.

For passenger cars parked on public streets, standard Seattle Municipal Code rules continue to apply including the general citywide 72-hour maximum parking limit, existing residential/timed parking zones, and standard 24-hour warning notices prior to impoundment.

Supporting ordinances update the Land Use Code for vehicle storage, expand leasing caps to 100,000 square feet for safe lots, modernize the definition of “junk vehicles” to streamline blighted vehicle removal, and fund eight city staffing positions.
Officials say the package is intended to match improved regulation and enforcement with expanded services to help people who live in vehicles of all types in the city.
Approximately 27% of individuals experiencing unsheltered homelessness in King County live in vehicles including cars, vans, buses, RVs, and travel trailers.

Concerns the new Seattle program will push vehicle homelessness outside the city will mean stricter rules across the region. King County Council Vice Chair Reagan Dunn is proposing new regulations for roads and public rights-of-way in unincorporated King County “to prevent Seattle’s homelessness crisis from spilling into neighboring communities.”

paras: I think I’ve developed a crush on my wife’s ex. I’m in my forties and my wife is older than me. We’ve been together for fifteen years. We are both women. Before we dated each other, we dated men exclusively. She had told me a lot about her ex before me. They were together for six years and lived together, so he came up a lot. I was really insecure at the beginning of our relationship and felt really jealous of him. As time went on, I became more secure in our relationship and I stopped thinking about him. They never spoke while we dated. That is until about two years ago, when he called out of the blue to say he was in town and asked if she wanted to meet up for dinner. We already had dinner plans so I told her to ask him to join us. The dinner was pretty awkward, as you could tell he was nervous. He cried at least once and kept asking us if we were happy in our relationship. He shared that night that he and his wife were in couples counseling for the second time. My initial reaction was to be put off by him and the whole experience — too much sharing — and I could still sense sexual tension between him and my wife. She wants nothing to do with him. However, recently I’ve been thinking about him and have realized I think he’s hot. I know he has a big dick. I would love to sleep with him but I don’t even know what he thinks of me from that one dinner. My wife has always said that I could open up our relationship if I wanted to sleep with someone else. She’s not interested in sleeping with anyone else but would be fine with me doing it as long as we discussed it first. However, I’m not sure she meant that she’d give her blessing for me to sleep with her ex. My questions:
1. What do I even do here? 2. Should I just leave it as a fantasy? 3. Should I bring it up to her? 4. Should I contact him? 5. Have I finally lost my mind?
Thinking Really Intensely About Novel Group Love Experience
1. Keep your mouth shut. 2. Yes, you should. 3. No, you should not. 4. Abso-fucking-lutely not. 5. Sounds like it.

Crushes are a kind of madness, TRIANGLE, and we’ve all been there — we’ve all lost our minds, some of us way more than once. Hell, I don’t think someone who’s never had an obsessive, all-consuming, wildly inappropriate crush can really say they’ve lived. And while it sounds like this crush only recently bubbled up, this guy has loomed large in your psychosexual imagination for a very long time. But just as you’re not the first person to lose their mind like this, you aren’t the first person whose jealousy transubstantiated into lust. (Yes, yes: We see you, aromantic people! You are valid! But even if you’ve never had a mad crush on someone , you’ve surely had a crush on something . Cinnamon rolls? Weighted blankets? Percussion massagers?)

And while it might help this dude to know your relationship isn’t perfect either — his ex’s partner has struggled with obsessive jealousy and now has a crazy-making crush on someone else — I can’t see how it would help him to know he was the focus of your obsessive jealousy and is currently the focus of your obsessive crush. As for the sexual tension you perceived between your wife and her ex, TRIANGLE, that sounds like projection. After all, you’re the one who wants to fuck this guy, not your wife, who says she wants nothing to do with her ex. And, I’m sorry, but there’s no way for you to act on your desire to fuck this guy — which, again, sounds like an eroticized fear — without getting your wife involved.
Luckily for you, TRIANGLE, crushes are almost always a temporary insanity. Like the jealousy that came before it, this too shall pass. Pray on it, masturbate about it, wait it out.

P.S. I’m such a contrarian that I can’t even resist contradicting myself: If you absolutely, positively must bring up the subject of fucking her hung ex with your wife (!), you could claim to have had an erotic dream about her ex and see how she reacts. Try to be neutral, bemused, and matter-of-fact when you mention your dream. (Don’t make the mistake I detailed in my response to Q6 here !) If your wife reacts with horror, drop it forever . If she sighs and says that she sometimes misses the sex and/or that big dick… you could continue to discuss him (maybe have one or two more dreams to goose the convo along) and see where it goes. But follow her lead, TRIANGLE, and be prepared to pivot to praying on it, masturbating about it, and waiting it out.

My 11-year-old granddaughter has discovered masturbation. She is in full-on puberty and she has her period but is very much emotionally a child. She uses the family percussion massager for self-stimulation and keeps it in her bed. No one is particularly concerned about the self-stim, but I am concerned about her use of the massager. It is not delicate stimulation and seems designed for back and shoulder massage. My question is, could it be harmful used on her genitalia? I’m thinking her delicate female parts may end up completely desensitized especially since it is used frequently. My daughter-in-law seems unconcerned and my son steers clear of that topic. What do the experts say?

I’m no expert, TMI, but lots of adults have told me about all the crazy things they used to self-stimulate when they first began exploring their bodies as kids, and almost all report growing up to be sexually healthy adults with fully functional/sensate genitalia. Maybe survivorship bias is at play here — I haven’t spoken to guys who didn’t survive putting their dicks in a vacuum cleaner hoses at age eleven, what with them being dead and all — but I’ve heard so many off-the-wall stories, from men and women alike, and I’ve always asked the obvious follow-up question: “Are you okay now?” (If someone tells me they used the family blender as a sex toy, I’m allowed to ask as many follow-up questions as I want.) And very few reported lasting trauma and/or loss of sensation on account of the banister railings, blenders, rolling pins, washing machines, cucumbers, personal massagers, etc., etc., etc., they experimented with as kids.

But I imagine more would’ve reported lasting trauma if their grandmother had known how they were masturbating and had decided it was her job to intervene. Also potentially traumatizing: their grandmothers writing to sex-advice columnists about the precise stage of puberty they were in (full-on is the most serious stage!), whether they were having periods yet, what the experts might’ve said, etc.

Here’s what you do: Say your piece to her parents — that’s a grandmother’s right — and then slowly disappear into the bushes . Worst-case scenario, your granddaughter grows up to be one of the many adult women out there who need the kind of powerful stimulation only a vibrator can provide in order to climax. Since there’s no way of knowing what percentage of those women conditioned themselves to need those powerful sensations during childhood explorations and what percentage would’ve needed those powerful sensations regardless, TMI, your best course of action is to stay out of it.

P.S. So, it was a woman who confided in me about sneaking into the kitchen at night when she was a teenager and swiping the blender — just the base, not the pitcher — and taking it to her room, where she would plug it in, turn it on high, and press the side of it between her legs over her sweats. Her mother found the blender in her bed on more than one occasion, and never once asked what she was doing with it… because her mother knew. This is anecdote and not data, I realize, but this woman told me she’s fine now, thanks, she doesn’t require a blender in order to come, and her mother eventually left a vibrator — still in the box — under her pillow.

P.P.S. I hope your daughter-in-law is talking to her daughter about sexual health, that she’s already told her know it’s normal for kids her age to explore their own bodies alone and safely and in private, and that your DIL has also told her that, right now, no one else should be touching her body. If she’s done/said all that, your DIL is doing great. Once you’ve verified the above, you could — one last time — express your concerns about your granddaughter using “the family percussion massager” to explore and then add: “Maybe you could leave a gentler gentler ‘personal massager’ on the same shelf where you keep that percussion monster. And now I’ll butt out!”

I’m a bisexual , 28-year-old man in a monogamous relationship with a 26-year-old woman. We’ve been dating for four years. My partner knows I’m bi and is fine with me using solo exploration to get that out, but recently, solo exploration isn’t cutting it anymore. I feel a very strong urge to be with a man again that at times verges on overpowering. My partner is not comfortable with an open relationship of any kind. I don’t want to cheat and lose a good relationship, but I’m also not sure how long I can hold out against these urges. Any advice is greatly appreciated!

paras: Our corporate overlords don’t oppose the Millionaires Tax: Or at least, they aren’t spending big to destroy it at the ballot, as they have done to similar income tax proposals in the past, the Seattle Times reports . The lack of oligarch backing means the petite bourgeois small business tyrants must fund the repeal on their own, and they’re being outspent by the big unions. I’ll have more on the why later, but in short, Washington’s major corporations can read the writing on the wall, and know that if we fail to tax the income of millionaires the progressive taxation movement will expand corporate taxation instead. And shifting your tax burden onto someone else is what tax reform is all about.

Prosecutor in Washington’s second-largest city reopens investigation into deadly police shooting after reporting by local media: You can tell it’s an election year because Spokane County’s incumbent prosecutor has reopened an investigation he closed two months ago into local cops who fatally shot a local man. The announcement comes only a few weeks after Spokane-based news outlet RANGE published texts from the officers, such as “So what’s the crime we were investigating yesterday? Unlawful discharge? Haha.”

The WNBA trans panic is a fake campaign amplified by a small network of money-grubbing influencers and pundits: Data analytics company GUDEA analyzed hundreds of thousands of posts on the subject over the summer, and found that only eight of them gained significant traction, and were pushed by influencers trying to make money. “If you take out the eight top posts, this [narrative] didn’t happen. Nobody would be talking about this,” GUDEA told Rolling Stone . So if you believe this nonsense, it is not an original thought—you were programmed by a machine, you live in The Matrix. I’m trying to free your mind, but I can only show you the door.

The WNBA might remain the only game in town for Seattle basketball fans: ESPN and the Seattle Times report the NBA expansion cabal has placed our fair city on the backburner once again, which is why you don’t get your hopes up about the return of a team named after vaporware that failed so spectacularly that it crashed the local economy and documentarians started making films about local child poverty.

Longview Daily News is the latest Washington paper we’re highlighting for trying to replace journalism with AI bullshit: The paper in owned by Lee Enterprises, one of the smaller of the bad national chains of local newspapers, and which you probably haven’t heard of unless you’re from Montana, where they own nearly every major metro daily, or what’s left of them after laying off almost the entire state press corps and selling their printers and buildings for cash. Lee Enterprises’ latest suicidal moneymaking scheme is publishing AI deepfakes and refusing to give their workers contract guarantees that they won’t be replaced by poorly-programmed machines. The Longview NewsGuild (part of the same labor union that reps Stranger workers, by the way) has been bargaining since July to get management to please just act like a normal newspaper.

They should have sent a cowboy: Klickitat County Sheriff Bob Songer is one of those libertarian LARPers who thinks they are the highest law of the land and make it everyone else’s problem. The “constitutional” sheriff, infamous for his literal posse, is retiring, and his potential successors are mulling how many of his far-right traditions they should echo to attract voters this election, Investigate West reports .

Why did we ever believe the Yakima grifter behind the world’s most famous Bigfoot footage? If you’re ever tracking a Sasquatch in Klickitat County and worried that bagging it across the county line will expose you to Skamania County’s fascist Bigfoot conservation ordinance, I have good news: Bigfoot is not real. Marq Evans’ new documentary Capturing Bigfoot exposes Washington man Roger Patterson’s famous Klamath River footage as fake by interrogating the man’s life as a stereotypical Pacific Northwest conman, Variety reports .

Hitler News: Declassified report shows CIA resettled Nazis in Canada: If you are an avid Tuesday morning Slog AM reader then you have been waiting with breath as bated as mine for the release of the “Rodal Report” after the Canadian judiciary cleared the investigation into how so many Nazis ended up in their country for publication earlier this year. “Nazi War Criminals in Canada: The Historical and Policy Setting from the 1940s to the Present,” as the report is officially known, was created in the 1980s when the Canadian government was forced to publicly investigate their Nazi problem, ending with a massive coverup. Read details of the CIA’s rat lines to Canada in the Maple .

US-backed Alberta referendum fails: Transplanting a bunch of Nazis into Canada wasn’t the end of US interference with our neighbors to the north. Alberta has long been the farthest right member of the confederation, evidenced by—what else—one of those aforementioned resettled Nazis becoming the president of the province’s long-ruling Tory party. It’s always been the most American-inflected province, too, due to high US immigration, as well as the influence of the Houston-based oil industry that runs the place the way Marco Rubio runs Venezuela from Mar-a-Lago. If the whole “a Nazi leads our ruling party” didn’t make the reality of Conservative rule in Alberta clear enough, leaders supporting the local independence movement to spite the Liberal prime minister (in the most charitable read) should tell you how serious these people are about providing for their constituents.

I thought Lance Oppenheim was the same guy as Joshua Oppenheimer, which means my expectations going into You Can See Everything were a bit off. I figured Nathan Fielder’s turn from comedic rehearsal to dark reenactment must have been influenced by Oppenheimer’s use of reenactment to interrogate the perpetrators of the Indonesian genocide of communists and Chinese in 1965-66 in his documentary The Act of Killing. But this is not true, because Oppenheim is not Oppenheimer, and I am a fool. articles.title: Tatiana Brown vs. Chipalo Street, the Matchup for State Senator for the 37th District
paras: In the race for Washington State Senate District 37, Tatiana Brown, a community organizer and the youngest co-chair of Washington State's Environmental Justice Council, says her career has focused on "answering the question of how do we actually shift decision-making power to our communities." She has secured healthcare access for immigrants and refugees in Virginia, and, most recently, piloted one of the first government-funded community assemblies at the Peoples Economy Lab.

Her opponent, Chipalo Street, a state representative for the 37th District since January 2023, works at Microsoft as a principal program manager for Copilot, the company's AI platform. Street sees his day job as an asset because "no one has [a tech] background in the legislature." Street is also a landlord who, he says, utilizes "progressive business practices" like rent control and pushes back on "the BS that comes out of the landlord lobby."

When the two squared off in the August primary, Brown received 25% of the vote, while Street garnered 74%. Ahead of their Nov. 3 race, the candidates spoke to the Emerald : Brown in person at Hing Hay Park, and Street over Google Meet. Both self-identify as progressives. Here's what they had to say about data centers, public safety, taxes, and more.

This year, one of the most contentious subjects for voters has been data centers . According to the Pew Research Center , half of Americans believe data centers negatively impact the environment, energy costs, and quality of life.

Brown wants to do more than just regulate data centers and AI because only focusing on regulation "disrespects our communities, [and] it really limits what ideas we're able to discuss." If elected, Brown hopes to pass a statewide moratorium on new hyperscale data centers and to study their environmental and community impacts.

When it comes to accountability and transparency, Brown says she will pursue a State Senate version of HB 2515, which would have required data centers to pay higher energy costs, comply with clean energy mandates, and shut down during peak demand. According to the Washington State Standard , lobbying from the tech industry, including Microsoft, led to HB 2515 failing to pass the House.

And Brown believes that Street, as a state representative who works at Microsoft, "has spent his career enriching Microsoft and not really being here for our community." Street says it's "frustrating to hear [Brown] try and allude to me working at Microsoft would change how I vote," and that he views promoting that idea as "disinformation."

Street, who voted for HB 2515, says his voting record is clear on regulating data centers: "I have been the person who's voted the most on data centers, and I've always voted to regulate them and will continue to do so."
When asked if Microsoft lobbyists have told him how to vote on bills, Street said, "No. I mean, they are just like any lobbyist who will come [to my office]."

One policy area where Brown and Street fully align is public safety, and the opponents believe that to reduce crime, the state should prioritize investing in communities rather than imposing harsher penalties.

That's why Street doesn't support a bill proposed by State Rep. David Hackney (D-Renton) that would mandate that juveniles receive law enforcement intervention after committing two gun offenses instead of four. "I have not seen any evidence that would get the outcomes that we want," Street said.

(At one point in the interview, Street said that Washington State has "one of the most punitive" sentencing guidelines in the country. But Dr. Jacqueline Helfgott, director of Seattle University's Crime and Justice Research Center, said that instead, the state is punitive when it comes to gun-control legislation, but "in the mid-high range" when it comes to firearm sentencing.)

Street wants more investments and services toward youth to help steer them away from taking part in gun crimes. He praised the recently opened Rainier Beach Playfield Skatepark , which received state funding and, Street says, helps "provide a sustainable path to real public safety."

Brown also took issue with a proposal to reduce the number of gun offenses — or "strikes" — youth commit before being incarcerated. "Public safety has to start with intervention programs and programs that actually invest in our youth," said Brown, "because those youth [who commit gun violence] are also victims."

For Brown, investments in supporting youth include funding for food security and efforts to keep people from being priced out of their neighborhoods. "Public safety has to start with … community cohesion and how do we actually show this community that we give a damn," said Brown.

On Nov. 3, voters will also consider Initiative 645, which, if passed, will repeal a State-legislated Millionaires Tax that would impose a 9.9% tax on every dollar of household income over $1 million. How does Brown feel about it?
First, Brown noted deep concern with wealth disparity, stating that "the top 400 wealthiest American families own more wealth than every single Black and Brown household combined."
(According to the Brookings Institution , a nonpartisan think tank, the top 400 American billionaires in 2020 had more wealth than all Black households combined.)

Because of how this disparity played out in the state, Brown supports the Millionaires Tax, as well as potential corporate and wealth taxes. But Brown doesn't go for lowering the tax bracket — until the tax system is fixed. "Washington State is currently funded by the working class," said Brown, "and until we can alleviate that burden, they should not have to pay another tax."

In his current role as state representative, Street serves as vice chair of the House Finance Committee, where he helped pass the Millionaires Tax. When it comes to a potential tax increase for low- and middle-income people, Street says "giving air to those ideas is not particularly helpful right now as the income tax is being challenged at the ballot."

Instead, Street talked about his "ideal tax code," which would have a "broad income tax that has progressive rates" and "a very low sales tax." He also discussed a progressive business tax, which includes a minimum tax, "so that companies, specifically large tech companies, cannot write off huge investments into infrastructure and avoid paying taxes."

Street and Brown also disagree on whether Washington should gerrymander the state to favor Democrats in Congress. ( Gov. Bob Ferguson has said that if Democrats hold a supermajority in the 2027 legislature, he would lead the charge to gerrymander the state to favor Democrats.)

Street said that "ideally, we would not [gerrymander, because] our nonpartisan redistricting commission is something to be admired." But in the current political climate, "we should do it, and we have to fight fire with fire in this case." Street said that Republicans' policies were "horrible," and he hopes those policies "backfire on them, and then we take this chance to implement nonpartisan gerrymandering laws across the country."

Brown says she would not vote to gerrymander the state because it "feels like a false or lazy solution towards actually building a very strong progressive movement for policy and system change." She continued, "I think there are very few instances where people who are vulnerable to a system … [were] actually the ones to benefit" from gerrymandering.

Throughout her interview, Brown referenced outgoing State Sen. Rebecca Saldaña, who is currently running for King County Council District 2 against Port Commissioner Toshiko Hasegawa. Brown says she entered the race in part because of "Saldaña [and] the work that she's done." Brown says she wants to be one of the "badass civil rights leaders and environmental justice leaders" who have recently held the seat. Even with her praise, Brown entered the race after Saldaña had endorsed Street.

As Street's interview wound down, he talked about the dynamics of Olympia and working to pass legislation. Noting that his three-year work on a bill to reform the estate tax failed while Sen. Claire Wilson's (D-Federal Way) efforts ultimately passed, Street said, "I am glad that I'm in the 37th and don't have to have my name on everything." He added, "I would rather do good policy work and get things done." To that end, Street says he can work with a diverse Democratic caucus, which his endorsements show.

Street says that regardless of who wins in November, he wants to see someone in the State Senate that "shares progressive values with the district," but he believes he's the only one who can "[turn] progressive values into actual policy."

articles.title: US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect
articles.author:
<name>Markus Schneider, Associate Professor of Economics, University of Denver</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/markus-schneider-2770471"/>
paras: The buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections may be affordability , but growing anger over inequality is behind the sentiment.

A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans – including 4 in 10 Republicans – believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this.

This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs.

I’m an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices – including taxation and public spending – enabled this 40-year rise in inequality.

Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%.

Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow . The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999.

These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data.

But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026.
Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories.

Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall . The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom.
Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive , often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats.

The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – including international studies – doesn’t back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth.

Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940 .

It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from.

Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership , allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash , usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares.

By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%.

Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed.

One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs.

The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil.

Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%.

This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “ A Brief History of Equality ,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.”
