articles.title: How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics
articles.author:
<name>Jordi Calvet-Bademunt, Research Fellow and Visiting Scholar of Political Science, Vanderbilt University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jordi-calvet-bademunt-1518048"/>
paras: With the U.S. midterms approaching, about 1 in 5 voters has asked AI chatbots about elections and politics, a recent survey found.

But many voters may not know that governments around the world increasingly shape what chatbots can say. And because many tech companies apply the same policies worldwide, the answers American voters get may be shaped by governments at home and abroad.

I’m a researcher at a nonpartisan think tank at Vanderbilt University, where I study free speech policy . In two reports published in 2025 and 2026 , my colleagues and I worked with global legal experts to examine how governments in 12 countries and regions regulate artificial intelligence. Our research shows that they often use existing rules , such as national security or anti-state propaganda laws, rather than new AI laws to control what AI models can say.
AI can cause real harm, from launching cyberattacks to generating sexualized images of children .

It’s important that governments tackle these harms. But, in our assessment, some governments use legitimate concerns like these as a pretext to control political discussion , particularly chatbot responses about those in power.

In 2024, an Indian journalist asked Google’s Gemini chatbot whether the policies of India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, were fascist . Gemini responded that some experts say yes . The government reacted by requiring official permission before “unreliable” AI models could be released . Although authorities later dropped this requirement , the case shows how terms like “under-testing” or “unreliable” can be used for political purposes.
India is not alone. China requires AI models to uphold “socialist core values.”

And in Turkey, a court blocked posts by Grok , the chatbot built into the social platform X, that allegedly insulted President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, founding father Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and religious values. Research by Turkish law scholar Yaman Akdeniz identifies the Turkish rulings as among the earliest documented cases of state censorship of chatbots .

Vietnam shows what such content controls can mean for dissidents, including those in exile. A Vietnamese court sentenced two activists , who live in Germany, to 17 years each in prison in December 2025 for spreading anti-state material. Prosecutors accused them of using AI to fake voices and images of Vietnamese leaders, illustrating how prosecutions can target political criticism .
Some of these government measures only affect people residing in their countries. Other statutes cross borders.

The European Union’s AI Act , adopted in 2024, requires any company offering AI tools in Europe, wherever it is based, to mark AI-generated content . Anthropic, for one, applies the marks globally because it has no reliable way to apply them by region . This is an example of the Brussels Effect , in which rules adopted in the EU end up applying elsewhere.
European rules also affect what chatbots say about politics.

In August 2026, the EU placed ChatGPT under the strictest tier of its Digital Services Act , Europe’s online safety rulebook. OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, now must assess and reduce the “systemic risks” of its service, including risks to elections, such as the spread of disinformation.

And the Dutch Data Protection Authority tested four chatbots before the 2025 national election and found that the political middle ground “virtually disappears” in their voting advice. It urged providers to “prevent their systems from being used for voting advice.”
These rules can be used to pressure platforms.

In 2024, Thierry Breton, then the EU’s top digital rules enforcer, reminded Elon Musk of his legal obligations before Musk’s live interview with then-presidential candidate Donald Trump on X, warning against the spread of “harmful content.”
Threats to Americans’ access to information do not come only from abroad.

In 2025, President Trump issued an executive order on “Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government.” It requires the AI models the government buys to be “truth-seeking,” ideologically neutral and not favoring ideas such as “diversity, equity and inclusion.”

“Truth-seeking” may sound like an objective, neutral term, but it can mean very different things to different people. Take media reporting: The president recently banned three news outlets from the White House for reporting “FICTION and LIES” and dismissed media polls as “fake.”
More recently, the Federal Trade Commission has suggested that AI companies that steer answers toward undisclosed ideological or biased objectives might break consumer protection law.

A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 8 in 10 Americans believe Republican and Democratic voters cannot agree on basic facts . In other words, as our report notes, government mandates to seek truth are often driven by ideological belief systems, particularly on political issues.

Meanwhile, dozens of states have passed laws restricting AI-generated political deepfakes. California and Hawaii , for example, are two states that have banned sharing deceptive AI content about candidates in the months around an election. U.S. courts have blocked both of those laws , citing the First Amendment.

What does this mean for voters? When you ask your chatbot about the elections, treat the answer as a starting point. Keep in mind that governments, both foreign and domestic, may try to influence the answer. AI responses should not replace your critical thinking at the ballot box.

articles.title: Are partisan politics even changing up our accents? They just might be, y’all
articles.author:
<name>Valerie M. Fridland, Professor of Linguistics, University of Nevada, Reno</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/valerie-m-fridland-1351277"/>
paras: With the midterms fast approaching, communicating just the right message has been top of mind on all sides of the political aisle.

Whether that message drives home a lack of affordability as gas, food and home prices surge or stokes fears about the rise of communism in the American heartland , Democrats and Republicans are spending a lot of time thinking about what to say.

But as a linguist who studies the impact of accents on the way people are perceived, I believe how politicians and voters say what they say might be just as important as the words they use in understanding the social consequences and linguistic changes resulting from the political divides that are growing between us.

If there is one regional American accent that has long endured on the lips of its speakers – as well as in the minds of listeners beyond the region – it’s the Southern accent. From North Carolina through Texas and pretty much all states in between, the so-called Southern drawl has long been emblematic of a distinct culture found in the South .

Yet, in the urban South, recent linguistic research finds that the drawl’s most salient features are starting to fade on the lips of young speakers . Fewer “pins” are merged with “pens,” and pronunciations such as “far” for “fire” or “say-ud” for “said” are becoming rarer.

While linguists have been busy trying to understand this trend, political scientists have been measuring how different accents perform on the campaign trail. The verdict? Southern accented candidates are generally heard as more conservative than those without a Southern accent, particularly to Democratic listeners.

Putting these findings from linguists and political scientists together, alongside a spate of studies examining correlations between voting patterns and vowels, hints, I believe, that the increasing conservative-liberal divide in American politics just might be the key to understanding what’s driving the decline of the drawl in the urban South.

The traditional Southern accent has no shortage of stereotypes: From positive, friendly, country and down-home vibes to negative, backward, uneducated and lazy tropes, the accents of William Faulkner, Bill Clinton and the hillbilly Clampetts have weathered it all.
The reality, of course, is that the Southern accent is not some incorrect version of a national standard but instead a historically separate and unique dialect – or, more accurately, set of dialects.

As explored in my recent book , this dialect formed from linguistic variation that came in with colonial-era settlers from different places and stations. The incipient differences increased after the Civil War intensified hostilities and cultural differences between the North and South.

The association with “countryness ” often triggered by a Southern accent grew out of this region’s agricultural past and its related cultural folkways. But what “country” has come to mean relies largely on stereotypes about what a country lifestyle involves . They include things like hunting, gun ownership and less socially progressive views – often arising from media portrayals of and beliefs about the South.

As the South has become more and more industrialized over the past half-century, these social meanings associated with the accent’s use now highlight a disconnect between its new urban vibe and its older, traditional rural one.
As rural vs. urban ideological and political divides in the U.S. have intensified, so has using symbolic means to signal this opposition.

Pickup trucks emblazoned with American flags and country music have become politicized . The white Southern accent, by virtue of its association with more rural traditional values, has also become emblematic of a conservative political identity not all modern Southerners share.

Recent linguistic research has compared voters in the South who had strong Southern accents to those with weaker ones, mainly measured through their use of a set of unique Southern vowel pronunciations , such as saying “bay-ud” for “bed” or “rawed” for “ride.”

It turns out that those holding more right-leaning positions and voting Republican in previous presidential elections used significantly more Southern vowels than those with more left-leaning positions who voted for Democrats. Three separate studies in Georgia , North Carolina and Tennessee discovered the same relationship between degree of Southern accent and political conservatism or liberalism.
The takeaway from these studies is that conservatism itself is embodied in a strong Southern accent.
The pronunciation of one’s vowels has become a barometer of how one’s beliefs and values fit within the old vs. new South.

Conservative ideologies and politics have become enmeshed with “country” speech and lifestyles. Young urban Southerners who don’t identify with these traits might be moving not so much away from Southern identity itself but rather specifically from this rural conservative identity it is often associated with.

Of course, other factors are also playing a role in the decline of the Southern accent in cities, such as heavy migration by non-Southerners to the region and greater interaction with people from other dialect areas via social media.

Outside the South, interestingly, recent research has found a greater embrace of Southern accent features, emerging in particular among those in rural areas where traditional lifestyles and, often, more conservative views are embraced. For instance, in a small, rural town in Ohio , speakers who identified themselves as more drawn to country lifestyles showed use of vowel features – such as saying “baa” for “bye” – more associated with the South.

So, in this circuitous and indirect way, vowels have become the latest players in partisan politics: Democratic Southerners wanting to distance themselves from the ideological and political climate associated with the rural South are moving away from its unique vowels. More “traditional” or conservative-leaning speakers continue to embrace them.

The real casualty in this particular battleground might be the obscuring of a larger culture, practice and community that the Southern accent has long represented for those who are automatically – and often erroneously – assigned a politicized identity just by the sound of their voice.

articles.title: Are transgender sports bans really about protecting women? Survey data tells a different story
articles.author:
<name>Tatishe Nteta, Provost Professor of Political Science, UMass Amherst</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/tatishe-nteta-1515087"/>
paras: Relatively few transgender athletes participate in high school and collegiate sports . Still, since 2020, 27 states have passed laws banning them from participating in sports based on their gender identity.

Just weeks after his second inauguration in 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order prohibiting transgender women and girls from participating in women’s sports in K-12 schools, colleges and universities that receive federal funds. Supporters of these bans often argue that they protect women and girls from unfair or unsafe competition. As Trump said at the signing ceremony: “we will not allow men to beat up, injure and cheat our women and our girls.”

WNBA star Sophie Cunningham offered a similar rationale in a July 2026 ESPN profile : “I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”

These statements suggest that those in favor of bans are motivated by their admiration for female athletes . But are Americans with more positive views of women and women’s sports more likely to oppose transgender women competing in women’s sports?

We are political scientists who study public opinion toward transgender Americans . To understand how attitudes about gender shape Americans’ views on policies that adversely affect the rights of transgender Americans, we asked 1,000 American adults about their support for restricting the participation of transgender athletes in sports. We also asked about their feelings toward women as a group, their endorsement of sexist stereotypes and their attitudes toward policies that promote gender equity, such as Title IX , the law requiring schools that receive federal funding to provide women and girls with equal opportunities to participate in athletics.

Our survey found significant public opposition to transgender athletes playing on teams that match their gender identity. When asked whether they “support or oppose a bill that prohibits transgender youth from joining school-sponsored sports teams that match their gender identity,” about half of respondents supported the restriction.

But admiration and support for women do not translate into greater support for excluding transgender people. In fact, individuals with the most negative views of women and gender equality are the most likely to support these bans.

We asked respondents to rate how they feel about women on a scale from 0 to 100. Researchers have used this tool, known as a feeling thermometer , for decades to measure how Americans feel about different groups, including people of color, gay and lesbian people and members of the opposite political party. Among respondents with the most positive views of women, 45% supported restricting transgender sports participation; among those with the most negative views of women, 58% supported restrictions.

We also tested whether more sexist views predicted support for these bans. To measure sexism, we asked respondents how much they agreed or disagreed with three statements about women: “Women seek to gain power by getting control over men,” “Women are too easily offended” and “Women exaggerate problems they have at work.” Social scientists commonly use these questions to measure “hostile sexism,” a set of stereotypes in which women are portrayed as incapable, manipulative and controlling. Among the least sexist respondents, 28% supported banning transgender people from sports matching their gender identity; among the most sexist, 79% did.

If admiration and support for female athletes drive support for prohibiting transgender women from participating in women’s sports, then those who favor Title IX should also favor bans. Instead, 43% of Title IX supporters favored restrictions, compared with 70% of Title IX opponents.

Our findings – that negative attitudes toward women and opposition to Title IX predict support for banning transgender women from sports that match their gender identity – hold even after accounting for other factors like partisanship, ideology and demographic characteristics.

The debate over transgender athletes is often framed as a matter of protecting women . Our findings complicate that narrative: People with the most negative attitudes toward women – and toward policies that protect women’s sports – are the most supportive of banning transgender women from women’s sports.

That does not mean that everyone who supports a ban is motivated by hostility toward women. But the consistency of these findings makes it difficult to accept that protecting women is a primary reason why Americans support these restrictions.

paras: Local school boards and district administrators typically determine how public schools are run. If students are not meeting basic academic standards, though, state governments sometimes step in and take over the day-to-day operations of entire school districts.
Since 1989, state officials have been appointed to temporarily replace elected school boards and superintendents in more than 100 districts across at least 22 states.

Texas has used takeovers more than most. Since 2015, the state has temporarily stepped in to run eight districts. A Texas law allows the state to take over for at least two years if one or more schools within the district has poor academic performance for five consecutive years.
Fourteen additional districts in Texas are now at risk of a takeover .
As an education professor at the University of Texas at Arlington, I often evaluate educational policies and interventions .

As part of this work, I teach a class on evaluating evidence for whether initiatives live up to their claims. Based on my research, Texas taking over school districts is not always helping the students there.
When a state takeover occurs, the state appoints a replacement school board, rather than holding an election. It also appoints a superintendent instead of allowing the district to hire one.

In October 2025, the Texas Education Agency announced that it was appointing a new school board and superintendent for Fort Worth Independent School District , one of the largest school districts in Texas.
Approximately 82% of students in this district live in poverty.

Marissa Sanchez , a mother with three children in Fort Worth public schools, told local station NBC 5 in October 2025, “these people that don’t know our communities, don’t know our students, what kind of representation will they bring, because we will no longer have a say in our local representative decision-making.”
Fort Worth’s school district had over 1,000 teachers announce their resignation during the 2025-26 school year after the announced state takeover – up 58% from the previous year .
It costs between US$11,000 to $20,000 for every new teacher to be recruited, trained and put in the classroom. That does not include salary, health insurance or other standard employment benefits .

Only 12% of Texas schools with 80% to 100% of the student population living in poverty achieved an A performance grade during the 2024-2025 school year . Meanwhile, 67% of Texas schools with a 0% to 20% poverty rate achieved an A grade, according to the Texas Education Agency .

Similarly, while 6% of students at schools with a majority-Black student population earned A’s, 16% of students at Hispanic-majority schools earned A’s. This compares with 35% of students at majority-white schools who received A’s.
At the eight Texas districts that the state has taken over – and the 14 currently at risk for a takeover – more than half of students who attend are eligible for free or reduced lunch.

And at the large districts that have been taken over, such as Houston and Fort Worth, more than 8 out of 10 students live in low-income households. A majority of students there are Black and Hispanic.
When states take over school districts, student enrollment typically declines. Staff turnover, meanwhile, increases.

Teacher attrition – meaning teachers who left the profession – increased by 48% during the first two years after the 2023 Houston takeover compared with the five years before. Almost 5,000 teachers left during the first year of the takeover, and another 3,300 left in the second year.
Principal turnover also increased dramatically in Houston, with 177 changes across 274 schools since 2024.

In 2023-2024, less than a year after the takeover, Houston had over 1,000 teachers not certified to teach. A year later, it had over 2,000 uncertified teachers because of a state law that allows teachers to waive the requirement that all teachers are licensed in certain cases.

Since the start of the takeover, about 21,000 fewer students will attend Houston public schools in 2026-2027, costing the district about $190 million in state funding . Many of these students are simply attending nearby schools that are not part of Houston Independent School District.
Takeovers work, according to Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath .
“In every single intervention, the results were higher, or at least no worse after the board of managers was placed than before,” Morath told the Fort Worth Report in September 2025.
But national evidence suggests otherwise .

A recent study of school takeovers nationwide concluded that takeovers, on average, do not improve student achievement. Rather, they are usually immediately disruptive to students’ reading achievement.

University of Texas at Arlington graduate students Veronica Erives, Nasja Aude, Jaclyn Foster and Cole Davis and I examined two Texas school districts, Shepherd and Marlin, in the spring of 2026, in forthcoming research.

Marlin Intermediate School District, a small-town district in central Texas, has about 800 students, 99% of whom live below the poverty level. Approximately 61% of the students there are Black, 31% Hispanic and 6% white.

The state took over Marlin schools in 2017, following five consecutive years of failing performance grades. In 2019, Morath extended state oversight of Marlin following continued low academic performance.

At the time of its takeover a few years later, in 2020, Shepherd Intermediate School District served approximately 2,000 students across four rural campuses in southeast Texas, with 71% of students considered economically disadvantaged.
The district’s student population was approximately 56% white and 35% Hispanic, making it one of the few predominantly white districts in Texas to experience a state takeover.
In both Shepherd and Marlin, teacher turnover continues to be a problem years after the takeover.
Comparing year-to-year performance at these districts is difficult, due to a redesign of the state’s standardized testing program in the 2022–2023 school year.
The Texas Education Agency explicitly notes that scores from 2023 onward cannot be directly compared to older test data.
There is a way, however, to sort of standardize the “approach grade level” percentages by comparing them to the state percentages. This has the effect of controlling for yearly changes in the tests.

For Marlin, my analysis shows, the percentage of third graders who approached grade level for reading in 2016 – one year prior to the state takeover – was 41%. This compares with 73% of third graders in Texas who were reading at this level in 2016. For third grade math, Marlin’s score in 2016 was 29%, compared with 75% for the state that year.

By 2019, two years into the takeover, 44% of third graders were approaching their grade level for reading, and 51% of them were doing the same for math, compared with the state averages of 78% on reading and 78% on math.

And in 2025, while 55% of third graders in Marlin schools were reading at grade level, just 40% were completing math questions at grade level. This compared with the state’s 74% and 74% averages that year, respectively. So, slight improvement in reading, none in math, and still way below the state averages.

For Shepherd, 56% of third graders approached grade level for reading in 2018, one year prior to the state takeover. This compared with the state average of 77%. For third grade math, 57% of Shepherd students were approaching grade level, compared with the state’s 78% average in 2018.
By 2025, the percentages for third grade reading and math were 56 and 50, compared with the state’s 77 and 71, respectively. No gains to speak of.
Similar trends exist for seventh grade reading and math.

articles.title: I’m a Philly forensic psychologist who has conducted dozens of psychopathic evaluations – here’s why an evaluation of R.C. Horsch in the ‘80s didn’t identify him as a possible psychopath
articles.author:
<name>David DeMatteo, Professor of Law and Psychology, Drexel University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/david-dematteo-2770324"/>
paras: Seven missing women have been linked to the house that was shared by 44-year-old Eugene Horsch and his late father, Raymond “R.C.” Horsch, in the Olney section of Philadelphia.

With five of the seven women feared dead, Philadelphia police and the FBI are conducting a massive investigation of the home . Law enforcement has said Raymond Horsch, who died in 2025 at the age of 82, is the suspected killer . Eugene Horsch has not been charged with any homicides or missing-person offenses related to the missing women.

The Horsch house investigation raises questions about serial killers and whether mental health professionals can identify a person at risk of becoming one. The early identification of psychopathy can potentially prevent an escalation of antisocial behavior .

As a forensic psychologist , I conduct psychological evaluations to help courts make decisions when someone’s mental health is relevant. I’ve conducted hundreds of forensic psychological evaluations, including dozens with individuals with psychopathic characteristics.

I’m not surprised that a previous psychological evaluation of R.C. Horsch, done in the mid-1980s, did not identify him as a potential psychopath. That’s because reliable tools for identifying psychopathy were not available at that time.

Psychopathic personality disorder, or psychopathy , is not an officially recognized disorder in the current version of the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders , or DSM. This is the primary diagnostic resource used by mental health professionals in the United States.

Although a version of psychopathy was included in prior editions of the DSM, more recent editions have eliminated the diagnosis. This is because of the difficulty in assessing some of the emotional characteristics of psychopathy.

Instead, the DSM includes a diagnosis for antisocial personality disorder , which focuses primarily on the behavioral aspects of psychopathy. Psychopathy is generally considered to be a more extreme variant of antisocial personality disorder.
While psychopathy is no longer in the DSM, it has been vigorously researched and written about for decades.

It is characterized by a distinct group of personality, behavioral and emotional traits. It has been defined in slightly different ways over the years, but some of the traits commonly associated with psychopathy include pathological lying, extreme narcissism, shallow affect, impulsivity and lack of empathy and remorse.
Psychopathy is also characterized by a persistent pattern of antisocial or manipulative behaviors. These can range from infidelity and intimidation to aggression and extreme violence.

The link between serial killers – individuals who kill several people in separate, unrelated events over a period of time – and psychopathy is not new. Several well-known American serial killers, including Ted Bundy and Jeffrey Dahmer , are suspected to have had psychopathic personality disorder .

To be clear, most individuals with psychopathic personality disorder are not serial killers. In fact, people with psychopathic characteristics can be found among corporate executives , elected officials and attorneys .
But some traits associated with extreme psychopathy, including the ability to engage in violent behavior with little remorse or guilt, are typically found among serial killers.

Given that psychopathic characteristics are common among serial killers, one might wonder: Can mental health professionals identify psychopathy when conducting a psychological evaluation and possibly thwart a future serial killer?

Mental health professionals are frequently asked to conduct evaluations of people involved in the criminal justice system who’ve been accused or convicted of serious crimes. For example, we might evaluate someone to help a court determine whether the person is competent to stand trial, or whether they should be found not guilty by reason of insanity.

Identifying whether a person has psychopathic characteristics may also be relevant to how a court sentences them after conviction. Individuals with more psychopathic characteristics typically present a higher risk for future criminal behavior . As such, because of the discretion given to judges and juries when it comes to sentencing in most states, courts are more likely to give a longer sentence because of the increased risk to public safety.
One of the most widely used psychopathy assessment tools, the psychopathy checklist-revised , or PCL-R, has been the subject of tremendous research over the past few decades.

Most studies find that the PCL-R can reliably identify psychopathic characteristics in both research and clinical settings. Individuals with higher PCL-R scores are more psychopathic and, therefore, at higher risk of engaging in future criminal behavior .

In 1985, R.C. Horsch was convicted in federal court of charges related to counterfeiting and methamphetamine manufacturing. As part of the federal sentencing proceedings, he underwent a lengthy psychological evaluation, which the Philadelphia Inquirer obtained through a federal records request.

The psychologist described Horsch as “ grandiose, mistrustful, suspicious and excessively controlling ,” and noted that he was “consumed by anger.” He concluded that Horsch likely had bipolar disorder and paranoid personality disorder.
The psychological evaluation found that Horsch had several characteristics associated with psychopathy, but he was not identified as psychopathic. Why?

One answer is that the tests used to identify psychopathic characteristics had not yet been developed in 1985. Although a precursor to the PCL-R was developed in 1980, it was not commercially available, and the PCL-R was not commercially released until 1991. Other psychopathy assessment tests were not developed until after the PCL-R.
An astonishing level of research regarding psychopathy has been conducted since the early 1990s.

Some research has found that the introduction of psychopathy evidence in both American and Canadian courts has increased dramatically over the past few decades. In these cases, psychopathy evidence is primarily used by the prosecution to argue for a more severe punishment of a convicted defendant.

There is also evidence that psychopathy evidence is being inappropriately relied on in death penalty cases . The PCL-R has not been proven to predict violence among inmates on death row or in highly restrictive prison settings. However, it can reliably predict violence among inmates in less secure correctional settings and among individuals about to be released from incarceration.

Other research has focused on the brain structure and function associated with psychopathy. Studies have found that the brain region associated with thrill-seeking and impulsive behavior is larger among people with psychopathic characteristics, while regions associated with emotional regulation and fear processing are smaller .

Identifying psychopathic characteristics before someone engages in violence is the ideal. However, most psychological evaluations of people involved in the criminal justice system take place only after the person has been arrested or convicted.

But if a psychological evaluation is conducted after an individual has been arrested for or convicted of a less serious crime, or when someone is showing early signs of antisocial behavior, the identification of psychopathic characteristics could help courts and treatment providers intervene before there is an escalation to violence.

articles.title: ‘Don’t wait for somebody else to fix it’: T-Mobile exec Deeanne King on cutting CO2 and costs
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: When Deeanne King came to the Pacific Northwest in 2020 — relocating from Kansas after Sprint merged with Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile — she fell in love with the region’s natural beauty. In her role as executive vice president and chief people officer, she also helps lead sustainability efforts for the telecom giant.
“The outdoors is my happy place,” King said. The region’s lakes, inland sea and trails, she added, are “a good reminder of what we’re all working to protect.”

T-Mobile has been ranked among the greenest companies in the U.S and globally. It’s making notable progress toward climate goals at a time when numerous corporations are scaling back or abandoning their carbon targets.
Keep reading to learn more about King’s sustainability journey. Her quotes have been edited for clarity and length.
What gives you the most hope for the planet?

People. Hands down. I get to work with some incredibly smart, curious, and committed people, and one thing I’ve learned is that when you put a hard problem in front of people who care, they find a way. They challenge the status quo, they try something new, they learn, and they keep going. I’ve never seen our teams walk away from a problem because it was hard.

I’m also encouraged by the growing recognition that sustainability and good business can, and should, go together. Building more efficiently, using resources more thoughtfully, and reducing waste can make a business more resilient while also being better for the planet. Those things don’t have to compete.

And I see that mindset in our employees. People want their work to matter. They want to contribute to something bigger than themselves. When you combine that sense of purpose with ingenuity and a willingness to work together, I think there’s tremendous reason for hope.
What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?
I’ve gotten much more intentional about cutting down on single-use things, and my reusable water bottle is probably the simplest example. It goes everywhere with me now.

It sounds small, but I think that’s actually the point. Once you make one change part of your routine, you start noticing other opportunities: what you throw away, what you reuse, what you buy, and what you probably didn’t need in the first place. Those small choices add up.
Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I’d choose Chief Sustainability Officer Kara Hurst at Amazon. T-Mobile joined Amazon and hundreds of other companies in signing the Climate Pledge, committing to reach net-zero carbon by 2040. And there’s something Kara has said about that work that really resonates with me: “We cannot go at this alone.”

I couldn’t agree more. The biggest challenges we face aren’t going to be solved by one company, one industry, or one really smart person. We have to find common ground, share what we’re learning, and be willing to work together toward something bigger than any one of us.

I’d love to sit down with Kara and compare notes on what’s working, where we’re getting stuck, and where companies like ours can work together to move faster. And knowing me, we’d probably end up talking about people and leadership too, because ultimately, ambitious goals only become real when you have people who are willing to question how things have always been done and figure out how to get there.
What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Making sustainability practical. Sometimes we gravitate toward the giant, breakthrough idea, and we absolutely need those. But there is also enormous opportunity in doing the basics really, really well and using data to figure out where small changes can add up to a very big impact.

Take buildings. They aren’t necessarily the first thing people think about when they think about climate innovation, but managing HVAC systems more intelligently produced nearly $5 million in estimated energy savings for T-Mobile in 2025. As of 2025, we have 132 community solar projects in our portfolio, providing an estimated lifetime total savings of $60 million in energy costs. You can reduce energy use, lower costs, and do something positive for the planet.
What’s one metric you watch obsessively as a sustainability leader?

I don’t know that I would use the word obsessively, but I absolutely believe in measuring whether the work is actually making a difference. One number I’m particularly proud of is that in 2025, T-Mobile’s total emissions were 50% lower than our 2020 baseline. That’s meaningful progress, especially because our business hasn’t been standing still.
The scope of the climate challenge is daunting — how do you approach this work?

You can’t let the size of the problem become the reason you don’t start. That’s true of climate change, but honestly, it’s true of almost every really hard problem I’ve encountered in my career. When something feels enormous, I focus first on what we can control. What’s the next decision? What’s the next action? What can we make better today? Then you keep going.
I’m also a big believer in being willing to learn along the way. Take smart risks, look at the data, listen to people, adjust and keep moving.
What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

As a mom, I think about the world we’re handing to the next generation. Of course I want my children, and someday, their children, to inherit a healthy planet. But I also want them to inherit the belief that when something matters, you don’t wait for somebody else to fix it. You figure out what you can do, you bring people together and you get to work.

articles.title: Housing Accountability Act Puts Tiny Beaux Arts Village in the Spotlight
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Changes to state law intended to broaden access to more affordable types of housing are reverberating in some unexpected places, including within Puget Sound's smallest jurisdictions. Last week, the town council in Beaux Arts Village – population 310 – met to approve a slate of temporary zoning changes, under threat of state sanctions and prompted by the 2025 Housing Accountability Act. While the vote was unanimous, the meeting included plenty of hand-wringing about the path the town had taken to get to that point.

Clocking in at just 0.17 square miles, Beaux Arts Village is a town entirely ensconced within the City of Bellevue, a pocket of narrow, tree-lined streets where golf carts are more commonplace than apartment buildings. Founded in 1908 as an artist's colony, the town's initial boosters drew residents with advertisements in the Seattle Times touting the fledgling community as "an expedition into the realms of Utopia." The town's primary amenity is a 1,100 foot stretch of beach, which only town property owners have access to as members of a separate, non-profit organization known as the Western Academy of Beaux Arts.

In 1954, Beaux Arts officially incorporated, to "protect the beach and the Village lifestyle," according to the town's website today. It had taken two years for Beaux Arts to reach the required 300-resident minimum necessary to be able to become a town, but just over seven decades later the population has only changed by six residents. Today, the median home value in Beaux Arts Village is $2.6 million.

In the decades since the implementation of Washington's 1990 Growth Management Act (GMA), the state-mandated growth plans in enclaves like Beaux Arts Village haven't traditionally been subjected to much scrutiny. But in 2025, the state legislature passed the Housing Accountability Act , empowering the Washington Department of Commerce to directly evaluate whether local jurisdictions are meeting the expectations laid out in state law when it comes to accommodating housing. Before that law was approved, the only avenue for a local Comprehensive Plan to be found inadequate was through a citizen appeal – though the state has sometimes taken the drastic step of making that appeal itself in extreme circumstances.

In January, Commerce announced that Beaux Arts Village had been selected as one of the first eight jurisdictions ever subjected to "selected review" under the Housing Accountability Act. As part of that review, agency staff have been tasked with determining whether all eight are in compliance with all aspects of the GMA, including new provisions that direct localities to plan for housing across different income levels – requirements that many cities have found vexing.

Beaux Arts' 2024 Comprehensive Plan was reviewed with a fine-toothed comb, and in June a preliminary report was issued to town officials that listed everything that needed to be adjusted to get into alignment with state law, in Commerce's view. That letter gave town officials their marching orders, and started the clock.

"We've been at it for nine months. We presented a Comp Plan that I think is in alignment with what everybody here will believe is keeping with what the village is, which has been much like the past three or four Comp Plans that we put together," Beaux Arts Councilmember Tom Stowe said Tuesday. "Commerce came in and shredded it, basically, and said that we couldn't do what we basically wanted."

Beaux Arts Village's share of Puget Sound's expected housing growth over the coming decades is not substantial. In fact, when King County handed out housing growth targets across all 39 cities and towns countywide in 2021 – an expectation of the number of new units to plan for through 2044 – the number was just one. Its neighbor Bellevue is planning for 35,000.

And yet the town's existing land use, intended to preserve a "tranquil, calm living environment" per the current Beaux Arts Village Comprehensive Plan, has presented certain challenges when it comes to growth plan compliance. Per a 2021 adjustment to the GMA known as House Bill 1220, Beaux Arts Village is required to plan for that one housing unit to be occupied by a household making 30% of King County's median area income or below – households that overall have the greatest difficulty finding housing.

30% of King County's median income is just under $40,000 for a family of two, and residents bringing in that little income cannot afford the single family homes that make up the vast majority of the town's housing stock, nor can they afford the backyard cottages that are allowed on those lots either.

To make it feasible to build at least one home that could be within reach to that future low-income household, Commerce recommended that Beaux Arts Village officials adjust zoning to allow some type of multifamily housing within their borders. Beaux Arts ultimately settled on the idea of creating a co-living "overlay." Co-living housing, also referred to as single-room occupancy (SRO) homes, provide the lowest rents even when built without any subsidy.

Though the idea of allowing six units of co-living housing just on one block of Beaux Arts Village was considered by the town planning commission, but counting on six property owners to build that specific type of housing would likely fall short of providing the necessary capacity. Instead, a proposal advanced that would allow co-living housing outside of the town's "erosion control hazard area" closest to Lake Washington.

The Beaux Arts Village planning commission deadlocked 2-2 on the idea of scaling back Commerce's recommendation to allow six co-living units on all lots in the overlay, but the town council ultimately did scale that number back to four. The fewer units allowed in the overlay, the less likely that it is that any actual co-living projects will get built – an outcome that did come up Tuesday.
"If we think this is about somebody coming in and building, nobody is going to build this," Councilmember Stacy Saal said.

As a town of its size, there is no Beaux Arts Village town hall – just a town mailbox. Town council meetings take place in a rotating councilmember's home, which is how a dining room and adjoining kitchen was transformed into a public meeting room last week for the monthly town council. Twenty to thirty Beaux Arts residents packed into the space, standing in the hallway or sitting on the floor as their elected representatives debated town matters, including whether to get in compliance with state housing law.

The big incentive for councilmembers to act and adopt the interim ordinance, which will expire February 4, was the stick included in the Housing Accountability Act. In addition to being disqualified for some state grants, cities and towns deemed to be out of compliance with the GMA trigger what is known as the Builder's Remedy .

A brand new provision in state law, the Builder's Remedy requires the approval of any complete building permit – no matter whether the underlying project conflicts with the underlying zoning for the site, as long as certain requirements for on-site affordable units are met. Theoretically, this could lead to a ten story apartment building in Beaux Arts Village, as long as a subset of the new units are kept within certain rents.

"If we don't do this tonight, as you all remember, the consequence is we go out of compliance, and the low income builder remedy kicks in, and any low income builder comes in and can submit plans that totally ignore our zoning code, they can come in and build whatever they want," Beaux Arts Mayor Aletha Howes the crowd in attendance on Tuesday. "The only thing they have to follow is setbacks and tree code. Everything else is blown out of water."

So far no jurisdiction has actually triggered the Builder's Remedy, with Carnation getting fully into compliance earlier this summer, and Bainbridge Island going the same route as Beaux Arts and approving a temporary ordinance a few days after Carnation. But in Beaux Arts just as there was on Bainbridge Island, some voices pushed for a more oppositional stance against state review.
During Tuesday's public hearing, local resident Dan Bridges urged councilmembers to take a more adversarial position.

"Well-meaning councils and boards sometimes lose sight of the fact that public agencies, state agencies – who we trust, like our parents, right? – they're still political agencies, and they have an agenda and they have a point of view. That point of view is not always the correct point of view," Bridges said. "Having an outside [entity] of coming to advocate for us would be helpful. And I would suggest if you haven't done that yet, you might consider doing that and not simply accept what some state agency is telling you. Only a judge is the one who decides the law."
For now at least, Beaux Arts Village has deemed the path of least resistance to be compliance.

"It is not that we are not receptive of what we're hearing," Stowe told public commenters. "It's that we quite frankly are up against them to comply, or they're going to go over us and say you have no authority and allow whatever zoning or buildings they say under the code – under Commerce's interpretation of the code, which has not necessarily been ours – and we have pointed that out that we don't read the law the same way they do."
As one of the first jurisdictions being put under the Housing Accountability Act microscope, Beaux Arts officials expressed clear frustration at the process of state review over the past few months.

They're not alone in that frustration. When members of the Carnation City Council held a public hearing with the Department of Commerce in July, many of the same concerns raised in Beaux Arts surfaced – about staff time, not an insignificant issue for a small city or town, and confusion over the purpose of the new law.

"Is this supposed to be helpful for us?," Carnation deputy Mayor Jessica Merizan asked Commerce staff at that July 9 meeting. "Because it really seems like you've pulled a lot of staff time, and the point seems to be saving staff time because these types of errors are happening. It just kind of feels like this is a teacher double-checking work, and not necessarily, these are areas of the community, in the region that perhaps need support, and we're here to offer that."

In Beaux Arts Village, Howes directly referred to what the Commerce department had been tasked with doing as "overreach" and called the idea of the state forcing local officials to spend scarce staff time on that review as an "unfunded mandate" that she called "bullshit."

"I am still pursuing the legislative changes in the next session with [Representative] Zahn, [Representative Thai], and [the Association of Washington Cities] is still pushing the seven legal arguments that we brought to them, and the seven other cities are also pushing to get those changes," Howes said, noting the temporary ordinance's four-month duration. "So if something moves during that time frame, then we can amend. If something doesn't move and it goes to final...you know, we'll see how the legislative session goes in '27."

Meanwhile, five additional cities and towns – including Woodway, Darrington, Gold Bar, Brier, and DuPont – are still in the process of coming into compliance, work that was spurred on by the Housing Accountability Act. And then next year, a whole new slate of jurisdictions will be announced.

articles.title: Get in line for a free preview of the Egyptian Theatre’s possible* future
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Want a preview of what the future of Capitol Hill’s Egyptian Theatre might be if a group of midnight-movie evangelists get their way?

While the sides say they are still working on an agreement for a long-term deal, the Classified Cinema pop-up screening folks are bringing another “secret movie” night to the Egyptian. The event will take place Tuesday, October 27th and it’s free: “First come, first seated.”

CHS reported in September on WFLM Seattle , the folks behind Classified Cinema, banding together to permanently reopen the Egyptian with a focus on repertory cinema, crowd favorites, forgotten titles, and the return of late-night midnight movie screenings.

WFLM and the E Pine theater building’s owner Seattle Central told CHS earlier this month they are still working out details of a hoped-for long-term lease for the venue that has been available for events but hasn’t been serving the public regularly since a major water pipe break damaged the former Masonic Temple in November 2024.
While the building was eventually repaired by the college, SIFF opted not to renew its lease after a decade operating the theater, leaving the screen mostly dark for the years since,

The WFLM group has been testing the cinematic waters at the Egyptian with events this summer including a sold-out screening of a documentary on Lenny Wilkens and “secret movie” collaborations and “physical media swaps” for Classified Cinema film geeks.

WFLM Seattle also has a special double feature planned for Hilloween with an October 31st Egyptian screening of Halloween at 7 PM followed by a 10 PM showing of David Cronenberg’s head-blowing Scanners .

articles.title: Central District House: Seattle’s first ground-up Social Housing project will rise at 24th and Yesler
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The Bird’s modernist angles will make way for 20 new affordable homes (Image: Seattle Dream Homes )
The first new affordable building the Seattle Social Housing Developer builds from the ground up will come in the Central District.

The Seattle Social Housing Developer has announced Central District House , its first construction project, will take place at 2402 E Yesler Way, marking a major milestone for the public development authority.

Plans call for a roughly $15 million, 20-home mixed-income development designed to Passive House environmental standards, with over half configured as two- and three-bedroom family units. Tenant selection will prioritize Central District residents and “people with current and historical roots” through the city’s Community Preference guidelines to help counter displacement.
Atelierjones is attached as the architect for the project.
The 20 new homes will be affordable rental units, permanently owned and operated by the public development authority.
SSHD has been making steady progress since its approval by the city’s voters in 2023.
CHS reported last winter on stronger than expected funding for the new authority giving the developer a head start in its mission to create and acquire affordable housing.

Officials said the voter-approved 5% tax on employers that pay any employee more than $1 million in compensation climbed above $115 million. The city began collecting the first Prop 1A payments from employers for the 2025 tax year in January. The tax had been expected to raise more than $50 million annually. A reported “10,000 applicants” signed up for the lottery for the developer’s first acquired property on Western Ave.

The income mix in Seattle Social Housing Developer properties is hoped to differ from previous affordable housing in Seattle by using mixed-income tier structure that spans from deeply low-income households up to middle-income earners, rather than serving low-income tenants exclusively.

The Central District and Capitol Hill have absorbed a large portion of the city’s most recent waves of redevelopment. In addition to market rate projects, major affordable redevelopment has reshaped many blocks.
The opening of Community Roots Housing’s Liberty Bank Building at 24th and Union in 2019 created 115 100%-affordable apartment units and street level commercial and restaurant space.
The Africatown Plaza mixed-use building at 23rd and Spring opened in 2025 as a 100% affordable, publicly funded project from Africatown Community Land Trust and Community Roots.

Meanwhile, developer Jaebadiah Gardner has held up his efforts with former church properties along 23rd Ave as examples a for-profit response can be part of balancing the city’s need for new housing with equitable growth in the Central District.
Other for-profit developments are also reshaping the area including the seven-story Acer House , the new “Afrofuturist”-styled development at the corner of 23rd and Cherry.
SSHD’s mission to serve the city will begin a few blocks east but its plans stretch beyond the CD.

Interim Chief Executive Officer Tiffani McCoy said the authority expects to announce a second acquisition before the end of year. By the end of 2027, SSHD plans to own more than 1,000 homes. “The ambitious pipeline is dependent on a successful low-interest bond issuance,” the authority said in its announcement.

The Central District corner has civic roots. it holds two cabin-like structures built by the late Washington State House Speaker Frank Chopp and his father, including “The Portal” and “The Bird,” a timber-framed home where Chopp’s daughter and community members lived. As the story goes, Chopp and his father bought the land at a public auction to build the structures as “ sort of a de facto Eagle Scout project .” The structures weren’t completed until the early 1980s.
Following Chopp’s passing in 2025, his widow, Nancy Long , offered the site to SSHD to advance his legacy as an affordable housing champion .
The property, just around the corner from the Douglass-Truth Library , is valued at $940,000, according to the county.
The modernist — but poorly aged — structures will be demolished to make way for the new building.
SSHD staff confirmed feasibility studies showed the 0.18-acre parcel is “very suitable for a Seattle social housing development with minimal risks to construction.”

During Thursday’s board vote, member Carl Nelson praised the deeper impact on residents: “A budget is an ethical decision, and the power to change that with your neighbors… I just want to commend the staff for what I think are really exciting first steps.”
Groundbreaking is scheduled for fall 2027, with completion targeted by late 2028.

articles.title: The AI Wars Come to Ravenna
articles.author: Harry Cheadle
paras: It seems likely that 2026 will be known as the year that AI broke through and became a mainstream political issue. Protests against data centers have swept the country , AI agents are launching cyberattacks against their own kind, and former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon became an overnight celebrity after quitting and warning the public that the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” AI is also worming its way into seemingly every facet of everyday life, from restaurant ads to social media to online dating . Depending on who you ask, the technology could make white-collar labor obsolete, usher in a kind of golden age, be more important than fire or electricity, or turn all humans into paperclips. It’s also central to a state legislative race in North Seattle.

Perhaps you’ve seen the paper ads stapled to telephone poles in North Seattle portraying a tiny person being menaced by a giant robot. “ANXIOUS ABOUT AI?” it asks. “Have you been waiting for someone to do something about it? DON’T WAIT ANY LONGER.”

This is an ad for Will Dreher, who is challenging longtime incumbent Representative Gerry Pollet in the 46th Legislative District, which encompasses North Seattle. Though there have been plenty of races in Seattle and elsewhere featuring a fiery progressive running against a more moderate incumbent, this isn’t one of those races. Pollet is generally regarded as a fairly left-wing legislator (though urbanists oppose his views on housing ). Rather, Dreher is running primarily because he doesn’t think the Washington State Legislature has moved quickly enough to regulate AI.

Dreher is a Harvard Law School grad who clerked for then-future Supreme Court justices Elena Kagan and Brett Kavanaugh. (The latter posting has become controversial in the election, with Dreher saying he didn’t get to choose who he clerked for; he denounced the conservative Kavanaugh after the judge was accused of sexual assault.) In 2019, he moved to Seattle and became a federal prosecutor, volunteering to work on the January 6 insurrection cases. But at the same time, he was reading about AI development and began to regard the technology as “on par with the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons,” he says. Dreher thought pushing back against AI was more important than his work as a prosecutor, which helped motivate him to join the law firm Keller Rohrback, where he’s helping sue Apple’s AI business on behalf of authors who claim their copyrights have been violated.

Dreher doesn’t have many pointed critiques of Pollet in particular (he’s praised Pollet’s work on education funding ), but thinks the Washington State Legislature as a whole has been slow to regulate AI. Lawmakers should have already passed legislation holding AI companies liable for untoward uses of their products, he argues, pointing to deepfake porn of minors as a particularly nasty application of the technology. He also wants the state to make it clear AI won’t replace certain government employees, like teachers, and enact job-protection measures more broadly. Other states like California and New York, Dreher points out, have passed a lot more AI-related bills, including some that try to address the “catastrophic risk” of the technology.
Pollet describes Dreher as a relative neophyte who is new to both the district and Washington politics writ large. “Will Dreher has never been involved for a minute in legislation,” Pollet says.

Despite his lack of experience, Dreher’s candidacy has caught the attention of people in the AI industry who would like the technology to be better regulated, and as a result, money has poured into his campaign—he’s raised over $304,000, compared to $214,000 for Pollet. Nearly 83 percent of Pollet’s donations come from in-state contributors, compared to just 20 percent for Dreher. As of publication time, about 36 percent of Dreher’s contributions, or over $112,000, come from people in the AI field, including researchers, engineers, and PhD students who have money to throw around and want to support pro-regulation candidates, even if those candidates are in low-profile races.

This is a trend nationwide, with cash-flush AI workers willing to fund obscure races in the name of pushing for greater AI regulation. OpenAI employees are even contributing to a PAC that is countering their executives’ spending. Individuals at these companies and others have funneled cash into a New York assembly race, a California Senate election, and a bid for governor of Alaska. All of those candidates have promoted strict AI regulations. This same dynamic is funneling money to Dreher.

“Will understands that the current AI regulatory regime is woefully inadequate, and that the largest AI companies need to be held to strong safety standards, to ensure that their products don’t pose a risk of catastrophic harm,” one of these out-of-state donors told The Stranger . “Many of my friends who work at AI companies are worried about existential risk from AI and have told me that they want their companies to be much more regulated, so that those risks don’t materialize. So, after chatting with Will, I decided to donate, and I encouraged some of my friends at AI companies to donate, too.”

The politics around AI regulation can get a little murky. Ian Mosher, the founder of a group called Ethical Tech Washington, says that some people concerned about AI are worried it could kill everyone, but others (including himself) view AI as a more normal technology that should be subject to a normal amount of government oversight. “This is a product that needs to have features that people need, that needs to be safe, that needs to be done in a way that is in alignment with our society,” Mosher says. “The people who are creating it need to be responsible stewards of that technology.”

Mosher recently wrote an op-ed for the Seattle Times that declared that “Washington is behind in the regulation of AI” and argued that the Legislature should pass bills ensuring AI companies would be liable for crimes committed by their systems and that these companies must get licenses to content used to train AIs. “Number of bills isn’t necessarily the best measure” for how well a state is regulating AI, Mosher told The Stranger . What he wants to see is “foundational AI legislation” that can protect consumers and the public from all sorts of potential harms. In his op-ed, he called for the Legislature to pass the People’s Privacy Act, first introduced in the State House in 2021, which would require companies to get opt-in permission from users to get access to their data. If that legislation was in place, he argues, it would be harder for corporations to create aggressive AI tools that take advantage of that data to, for example, set grocery store prices that vary by customer (a practice that just got banned in Seattle). Mosher isn’t endorsing either candidate in the 46th.

Pollet is no defender of the AI industry. He sponsored a bill regulating chatbots that passed this year . He’s also been a sponsor of the People’s Privacy Act, and blames opposition from the tech industry, which favors a weaker form of privacy protections (which he calls a “deepfake”), for its failure to pass. He also supports a moratorium on data center construction—as does Dreher and seemingly every other Democrat in town—and says he’s working with legislators in Oregon on an ambitious two-state proposal that would tax data centers in order to create a fund to help offset impacts from AI-related job losses. Oregon and Washington need to partner on this, he says, because “if you tax on one side of the [Columbia] River, they’ll just put the data center on the other side of the Columbia and get their electricity from across the river.” The Legislature hasn’t been ignoring AI issues, Pollet argues—the state just came out with a task force report recommending a slew of regulations, bills are being worked on, and progress is being made.

Win or lose, Dreher will likely give Pollet one of his toughest races since he took office in 2011. He typically wins with over 80 percent of the vote, but got 52 percent in the primary this summer, with Dreher claiming 31 percent and a third candidate, Ron Davis, earning 16. (Davis has since endorsed Pollet.) Pollet claims that Dreher’s AI industry donors will push him to back off taxing data centers. “When you’re funded by AI, and out-of-state people at that, they’re going to have access to you, that’s a reason for concern,” Pollet says. Dreher says that he has always supported a moratorium on data centers and that his AI-linked donors “have publicly called for many other regulations that would likewise hurt their companies’ bottom lines, like slowing or stopping AI development… So I have no reason to believe they oppose a data center moratorium.”

But whoever ends up representing the 46th, AI is going to loom over them—and everyone else in the Legislature. With the federal government’s unwillingness to regulate the new technology, tech-centric states like Washington have to step up.

“We have the opportunity to do things here in Washington,” says Mosher, with a legislature and governor’s mansion both controlled by Democrats who will have some motivation to address AI. “We have the right kind of constituency, the right kind of people to do it.”

articles.title: The Oatmeal and His Brother Built Jimothy’s Evil Dad to Haunt Bainbridge Island This Halloween
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: Sifting through the infosphere as I drafted Monday’s Slog AM, I was delighted to stumble on an Instagram post introducing Grimothy aka “Jim Reaper, Dark Lord and Father of Jimothy,” as his creators call him. Could this monstrosity have sown Seattle’s favorite short-spined raccoon whose likeness has been co-opted by sports teams, artisanal cutting boards, and the ugliest t-shirts known to man?

Grimothy, the broader-than-human-sized raccoon, is an animatronic Halloween installation. He is ghastly, but also beautiful. His red eyes glow, his bony arms flail—as if grasping toward Ballard, the hellscape his son has run off to—and his mouth of spiky teeth chomp towards cars and pedestrians in a quiet corner of Bainbridge Island.

This DIY freakshow (sorry, Grimothy) is the brainchild of brothers Matt and Bryce Inman. You may recognize Matt’s flair on Grimothy’s, um, essence. Matt is the cartoonist behind the card game Exploding Kittens and the webcomic The Oatmeal . Grimothy, while surely a haunted demon, bears a striking resemblance to Matt’s cute, but depraved style. Grimothy is currently living and snarling along Bryce’s sidewalk across from Cherry Avenue across from the Wing Point Golf & Country Club.
I had to know more. How did they put this together? Are they ready for a million visitors?

Inman told me in an email that he and his brother, Bryce, welded, wired, and “servoed” this monstrosity to something resembling life. I’ve reconstituted his responses, from him and his brother, below.
Is your brother ready for some foot traffic?
Matt: Last night (Saturday) at around 9:30 p.m., there was still a line of cars outside the house. We realized we’d turned the front yard into an all-hours tourist attraction.
What was the toughest part about building this?

Bryce : Getting the main ring structure welded together was tough because some steel rods are small and anything more than a tiny spot weld burns through and cuts the piece in half. So, if I made one small mistake Jimothy would implode on top of me. Also, the rag I used to clean the welder kept catching fire because of all the flying sparks, and Grimothy’s fur is super flammable. So generally speaking implosions and explosions were the hardest part.

Matt: Learning to work with servos—they are like little motors that make things move. Since my electrical skills are non-existent, Grimothy’s interior is a total hack job of bad wiring and electrical tape. Every few hours Grimothy has the robot equivalent of a stroke and half his face stops working. I then have to crawl inside him through a flap near the butt and jiggle a bunch of cables. It’s like an animatronic colonoscopy.

Matt: I directed my first short film, which debuted at film festivals across the country this year. It’s called My Dog: The Paradox , and it won Best Animated Comedy at the Portland Festival of Cinema and Animation. Other than that, I’m writing an all-ages science book that covers topics like neuroscience, black holes, wombat butts, and the mantis shrimp.
But mostly I’ve been spending time with my brother crawling in and out of a massive raccoon ass.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, October 19–25
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Amanda Manitach, Dave Segal, and Audrey Vann
paras: (LITERATURE) What can’t Barbara Kingsolver do? The bestselling author never misses, from her historical fiction classic The Poisonwood Bible to her 2022 Pulitzer Prize-winning sensation Demon Copperhead . Her most recent novel, Partita , follows piano teacher Livia Cable, who lives a peaceful, unassuming married life in the Tennessee countryside until an unexpected call from her ex-lover dredges up memories of trauma, tragedy, and her abandoned ambitions for a musical career. The book borrows both its name and format from a musical composition made up of dance movements. See Kingsolver discuss her lyrical work, her writing process, and the connection between art and life at Benaroya Hall, and don’t forget to bring donations for Ballard Food Bank’s food drive in the lobby, such as boxed mac and cheese, ramen, granola bars, oatmeal packets, cereal, and jerky. ( Benaroya Hall, 7:30 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) The son of legendary experimental saxophonist Anthony Braxton, Tyondai’s anything but a nepo baby. He’s earned his lofty status in underground music through his exploits in former best band in the omniverse Battles, who took math rock to rarely matched realms of rhythmic complexity, melodic whimsicality, and electronic tomfoolery. Braxton departed Battles in 2010 and since then has been focusing on a solo career that’s veered from vaulting orchestral and electroacoustic composition to abstract electronic music that could discombobulate Autechre fans’ neurons. On Braxton’s mind-bending new album, Splayed Werks , he conjures alien sound worlds that expand the vocabulary of electronic-music composition. This is a rare seated show at Vera, so STFU and listen. ( Vera Project, 7 pm, all ages ) DAVE SEGAL

(MUSIC) Astute local music critic and DJ Martin Douglas has coordinated another strong bill for his Trick Bag series. Olympia’s premier experimental-rock band, Debt Rag, puts punk and no wave in a cyclotron, resulting in concise, idiosyncratic songs that send diabolical heat and sparks through your sensorium. The trio’s music and lyrics possess the urgency and righteous rage that this perilous timeline demands. Check out their latest album, It Is Clear What’s Going On , for proof. Seattle’s Miscomings seemingly have absorbed the harsh lessons of the legendary No New York comp and transformed them into tracks that come at you like a herd of amphetamine-spiked porcupines, with bonus doses of Minutemen-like funk. Exhilaration awaits you. ( Sunset Tavern, 8 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL
MOPOP’s Icons of Pop Culture Gala With Salt-N-Pepa

(MUSIC) MOPOP’s Icons of Pop Culture Gala is probably your only chance to see the queens of hip-hop, Salt-N-Pepa, at a venue this tiny (unless you time-travel back to 1986). The duo, with DJ Spinderella, of course, will perform classics like “Whatta Man,” “Shoop,” “Let’s Talk About Sex,” and “None of Your Business” at the 250-capacity Sky Church. I really hope they also play a few songs from their criminally underrated 1997 album Brand New , which is rich with wordplay and glossy ’90s production, in the same vein as Lil’ Kim’s Hard Core . And look, I recognize that the $250 ticket price is no small thing, but if you’ve ever paid Ticketmaster/Live Nation hundreds of dollars, don’t think twice about supporting the MOPOP with their future exhibitions, youth education programs, and community initiatives. ( MOPOP, 8:30 pm, 21+ ) AUDREY VANN

(VISUAL ART) Melissa Messer describes her practice and work as “if Rothko’s daughter were obsessed with form.” I might add Albers to the mix: her approach to color is technical and clever and makes the eyeballs vibrate with a kind of ocular orgasm. But she’s right about Rothko, because her use of hue is almost spiritual in its ability to overwhelm. She is also a preeminent figurative painter, using the human body as an armature upon which to drape shades of deciduous greens, burnt orange, and acid gold. Beneath all that color, however, the figures hold their own. Messer paints to convey intimacy—the kind that comes from knowing the closeness of a body from innumerable hours of holding, caring, carrying, or resting. That feeling is palpable in the heavy limbs of the mothers, friends, and others who populate her canvases. They loom, stark and monumental, bodies dissolving into the color fields that surround them. ( Spectrum Fine Art, 12–5 pm ) AMANDA MANITACH
Mourning Sickness: ‘Elvira: Mistress of the Dark’

(FILM) Until recently, I had never seen Elvira: Mistress of the Dark , but rest assured I am making up for lost time. The 1988 cult classic revolves around everyone’s favorite goth horror hostess, Elvira (played by the iconic Cassandra Gay Peterson), who discovers her great-aunt Morgana bequeathed her a crumbling mansion in a small-minded town named Fallwell (likely a reference to conservative televangelist Jerry Falwell). The result is a delightful fish-out-of-water story, featuring relentless innuendos, a pink-dyed poodle named Gonk, a himbo love interest, a villain named Chastity Pariah, Tic Tac pie, and a bacchanalian picnic scene. This film was made in a lab for the gays—the slut-shaming and moral panic of the townspeople; Elvira’s fabulous drag; the film’s dedication to Peterson’s late best friend and makeup artist Robert Allen Redding, who died of AIDS; and of course, the fact that Peterson herself is sexually fluid and has been living her best queer life in Portland with her partner of 24 years, Teresa “T” Wierson. Who better to present this campy masterpiece than local queen Monday Mourning? ( Northwest Film Forum, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) Ken Ishii was the first Japanese solo electronic-music producer I got hip to, thanks to his 1995 album Flare dazzling me with its ingenious textures and dynamic rhythms. Throughout the ’90s, Ishii released a grip of phenomenal records in which IDM, techno, funky breaks, and ambient converged into fascinating hybrids. Shamefully, I lost track of him in the ’00s, but, whoa, Ken’s still creating and DJing like a madman, including a 2019 collab with Detroit techno legend Jeff Mills. Whether he’s performing his own cuts or spinning others’ in his wide-ranging sets, Ishii manifests a distinctive brand of dance-floor hypnosis. At Substation, he’ll be DJing, along with Cory Simpson, a prime mover in Seattle’s techno scene who heads the Depth crew. ( Substation, 7 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL
